anchor_text: It wears, sir, as it grows
summary: 'Wears' means 'wears out' or 'deteriorates' — the Painter says the world decays at the same rate it develops. The exchange is small talk, but the bleak answer plants a note of decline at the play's very opening.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'wear' vb. 3: 'to pass away, waste.' The phrasing also puns on 'grow' — the world ripens and rots simultaneously.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 4
Onions s.v. 'wear' vb. 3 covers the sense 'pass away, waste' and is a real entry; the claim is supported.
The 'wears out as it grows' reading is mainstream and well-supported; the passing note about a pun on 'grow/ripen-and-rot' is a defensible secondary layer, not an overreach.

anchor_text: breath'd, as it were, To an untirable and continuate goodness
summary: 'Continuate' means 'uninterrupted' or 'unceasing' — a word Shakespeare coins. The Merchant describes Timon as if he has been trained ('breath'd') by exercise into a goodness that never stops, like a horse conditioned for a long race. The praise is extravagant, already edged with flattery.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'continuate' adj.: 'continuous, unbroken'; the usage in Timon 1.1 is the sole Shakespearean example.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 13
OED does record 'continuate' adj. as continuous/unbroken and cites the Timon 1.1 line as a primary Shakespearean example; the claim is well-supported.

The horse-conditioning gloss on 'breath'd' is the standard editorial reading, and 'continuate' as 'uninterrupted' is uncontested; the observation that praise edges toward flattery is a reasonable dramatic note, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: If he will touch the estimate
summary: 'Touch the estimate' means 'meet the asking price' — literally 'reach' or 'match' the valuation. The Jeweller is hedging: the jewel is for Timon if Timon will pay what it is worth. 'Touch' carried a sense of monetary assay, as in testing gold's purity by rubbing it on a touchstone.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'touch' vb. 6: 'to reach, to come up to (a price or standard).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 18
Schmidt s.v. 'touch' covers senses including reaching a price or standard, and the touchstone/assay gloss is standard lexicography.
Both the monetary sense of 'touch' (reach/meet a price) and the touchstone assay association are standard editorial glosses on this line.

anchor_text: here is a water, look ye
summary: In gem-trade language, a jewel's 'water' is its degree of transparency, lustre, and clarity. 'Of the first water' (still in modern use) means the finest quality. The Jeweller is drawing attention to the gem's exceptional clarity as part of his sales pitch to Timon.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'water' n. 6b: 'the lustre or transparency of a diamond or other precious stone.' Cf. Othello 5.2.145: 'pearl ... richer than all his tribe.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 23
OED s.v. 'water' n. 6b does record the gem-trade sense of lustre/transparency; the Othello parallel citation is unrelated to the gem-water definition but the primary source is correct.
'Water' as gem-trade lustre/transparency is a well-attested technical term and the only sensible reading in context.

anchor_text: Our poesy is as a gum, which oozes From whence 'tis nourish'd
summary: The Poet compares poetic creation to resin that seeps naturally from the tree that feeds it — 'our gentle flame / Provokes itself.' The simile presents inspiration as organic and spontaneous, not laboured. The irony is that the Poet is here at Timon's house specifically to sell his work for patronage money, making the claim of pure inspiration self-serving.
detail: The Poet then shifts metaphor: unlike the gum's slow oozing, his current poem is like a spark struck from flint — and unlike a contained fire it 'flies / Each bound it chafes,' rushing past every limit. The two metaphors (organic seepage vs. unstoppable current) both argue that the Poet's genius cannot be contained or cheapened — a pitch dressed as modesty. The self-congratulatory tone is characteristically ironic in this play, where the 'artists' are shown as flatterers-for-hire.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'poesy': 'poetry, the art of making verses'; s.v. 'gum': 'resin oozing from a tree.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 27
Schmidt covers both 'poesy' and 'gum' with the senses cited; this is a standard lexical gloss with no overreach.

The gum-simile is correctly glossed as organic spontaneity vs. laboured art; the irony of a patronage-seeking poet claiming pure inspiration is a legitimate and widely-noted dramatic irony in this scene.

anchor_text: artificial strife Lives in these touches, livelier than life
summary: 'Artificial' here means 'produced by art' (not 'fake'): the Poet says that the skilled effort ('strife') in the Painter's brushwork ('touches') creates something more vivid than nature itself. This is the Renaissance debate about whether art can surpass its model — a claim that painting is paradoxically more 'true' than the original. The irony is that both these artists are about to flatter Timon with work that is not true at all.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'artificial' adj. 1: 'made by art, as opposed to natural'; s.v. 'strife' n. 3: 'effort, endeavour.' Shakespeare uses 'artificial' in this positive Renaissance sense also in A Midsummer Night's Dream 3.2.203.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 46
OED s.v. 'artificial' adj. 1 records 'made by art' and the MND 3.2 parallel ('two artificial gods') correctly uses the word in the same positive Renaissance sense.

'Artificial' meaning 'produced by art' (positive Renaissance sense) and 'strife' as skilled effort are standard glosses; the ut pictura poesis reference to the paragone debate is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: moves itself In a wide sea of wax: no levell'd malice
summary: 'A wide sea of wax' means his poem's subject moves freely across the whole wax writing-tablet — the Poet's draft is expansive and general, not pinned to one person or target. 'No levell'd malice' means no precisely aimed hostility: his poem does not aim at any particular enemy. 'Levell'd' comes from levelling a weapon or gun at a specific target.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'wax' (writing tablet); s.v. 'level' vb.: 'to aim, direct at a mark,' hence 'levell'd malice' = malice aimed at a specific person.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 55
Schmidt covers the wax-tablet and 'level' senses; both glosses are standard and well-supported.
'Sea of wax' as writing-tablet and 'levell'd' as aimed-weapon are the standard editorial readings for this notoriously difficult passage and hold up against the text.

anchor_text: Subdues and properties to his love and tendance All sorts of hearts
summary: 'Properties' is used as a verb, meaning 'turns into a property,' 'makes subservient to himself' — Timon's great fortune reduces all kinds of people to his possessions. The verb is Shakespeare's coinage and signals something troubling: even well-intentioned generosity can turn others into dependents.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'property' vb.: 'to make a property of, treat as one's own'; the earliest recorded use is this passage in Timon 1.1.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 67
OED does record 'property' vb. meaning 'to make a property of, treat as one's own' and the Timon passage is among the earliest recorded uses; the claim is standard.

'Properties' as a denominative verb ('makes into a property/possession') is well-attested and the troubling undercurrent of reducing persons to possessions is a defensible reading supported by the word-choice itself.

anchor_text: from the glass-fac'd flatterer
summary: 'Glass-fac'd' means mirror-faced — someone whose face reflects back whatever expression the person they flatter is wearing, like a mirror, so they seem agreeable at every moment. It is the Poet's description of the most servile type of courtier, the one who mirrors the powerful man's own mood back at him.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'glass-faced': 'reflecting like a mirror the face of one in whose company he is.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 68
Schmidt s.v. 'glass-faced' records precisely the mirror-face sense cited; the gloss is accurate.
'Glass-faced' as mirror-faced (reflecting the patron's own expression back) is the standard reading and is clearly supported by the courtier-as-mirror motif throughout the scene.

anchor_text: I have upon a high and pleasant hill Feign'd Fortune to be thron'd
summary: The Poet describes his poem: Fortune (the goddess of luck) sits enthroned on a hilltop, and a crowd of all human types scrambles up toward her. Timon is the one she summons to the top with her 'ivory hand.' The image draws on the classical tradition of Fortune (Latin Fortuna) as a goddess turning a wheel, lifting some to the summit and casting others down — a fable that exactly predicts what will happen to Timon in the play.
detail: The ivory hand is a detail of Fortune's iconography: in classical and Renaissance emblems she was sometimes depicted as white and smooth (ivory = pure luck, bloodless, unearned). Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (Book II) is the great medieval transmission of the image; it was available to Shakespeare through countless summaries, Chaucer's 'Monk's Tale,' and the Mirror for Magistrates. The Poet's fable is self-consciously meta-theatrical: the poem he is selling Timon is actually the play's own plot summary.

sources.name: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1–2 (Fortune turning her wheel and casting down her favourites).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 74
Boethius Consolation Book II prose 1-2 does contain Fortune's speech about her wheel lifting and casting down favourites; the citation spans the correct location.

Fortune enthroned on a hill with ivory hand is standard Renaissance iconography well-grounded in Boethius and emblem tradition; the meta-theatrical point that the Poet's fable maps onto the play's own plot is a legitimate and widely-noted interpretive observation.

anchor_text: Rain sacrificial whisperings in his ear, Make sacred even his stirrup
summary: The Poet describes the sycophants who crowd Timon's entourage: they whisper devotion in his ear as if offering a religious sacrifice, and they treat even his stirrup (the loop he steps into to mount his horse) as a holy relic. 'Sacrificial whisperings' and 'sacred' translate a patron's physical presence into something like divine worship — a precise image of the flattery-as-religion that runs through the scene.
detail: Helping a great lord to mount his horse, or kissing his stirrup, was a real gesture of deference in Elizabethan and Jacobean court culture. 'Rain' in the sense of 'shower down, pour' was common. The metaphor collapses the political (lobbies, dependents) into the religious (sacrifice, sacred), anticipating the play's consistent equation of wealth with godhead — and its later inversion when Timon is broke and the 'worshippers' vanish.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'sacrificial': 'of or pertaining to sacrifice'; s.v. 'stirrup': the mounting-loop as a conventional image of court servility.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 94

Schmidt covers 'sacrificial' and 'stirrup' but the specific claim that Schmidt glosses 'stirrup' as 'a conventional image of court servility' overreaches a standard lexical entry; no independent source is cited for the cultural-history claim about kissing the stirrup as Elizabethan court practice.
The 'sacrificial'/'sacred' language as flattery-as-religion is explicitly in the text; the stirrup as a real Elizabethan deference gesture is documented and not an anachronism.

anchor_text: When Fortune in her shift and change of mood Spurns down her late beloved
summary: Fortune's 'shift' is a change of direction — she turns her wheel, kicking away ('spurns down') the favourite she has just been raising. The Poet describes the second half of the fable: when Fortune abandons Timon, every follower who had climbed up with him abandons him too, 'not one accompanying his declining foot.' This is the de casibus pattern: a great man's fall proves the worthlessness of all around him.

sources.name: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 2 (Fortune's speech: 'This is my art, this the game I never cease to play. I turn the wheel that spins; I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend').

anchor_text: More pregnantly than words
summary: 'Pregnantly' means 'more pointedly, more clearly, with more force' — not referring to pregnancy in the modern physical sense. The Painter claims his thousand moral paintings demonstrate Fortune's cruelty more vividly than speech can. 'Pregnant' in Shakespeare regularly means 'full of significance, apt, telling.'

sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'pregnant' adj. 4: 'clear, obvious, telling' (of an argument or proof).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 106
Schmidt s.v. 'pregnant' adj. 4 records 'clear, obvious, telling' as a standard sense; the gloss is accurate.
'Pregnantly' meaning 'pointedly, tellingly' is the standard Shakespearean usage and is not confused with modern sense.

anchor_text: I am not of that feather to shake off My friend when he must need me
summary: 'Not of that feather' means 'not of that kind or type' — the phrase uses 'feather' as a metaphor for character or sort, as a bird is identified by its plumage. Timon says he is not the type to abandon a friend in need. The idiom sets up the play's central irony: his own fair-weather friends will do exactly that to him.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'feather' n.: 'kind, character, nature' (used figuratively for type of person, as 'birds of a feather').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 116
Onions s.v. 'feather' records the figurative sense of 'kind, character' and the proverbial 'birds of a feather' parallel; the gloss is accurate.
'Feather' as kind/type/character is a standard idiom and the gloss is accurate; the dramatic irony noted is well-supported by what the play then shows.

anchor_text: being enfranchis'd, bid him come to me
summary: 'Enfranchised' means 'freed' — liberated from prison, restored to the rights of a free person. Timon will pay Ventidius's debt and then summon him once he is released. The word comes from the legal granting of freedom (a 'franchise') and was used both for freeing a prisoner and for granting civic rights.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'enfranchise' vb. 1: 'to make free, set at liberty (a prisoner or slave).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 122
OED s.v. 'enfranchise' vb. 1 records 'to set at liberty a prisoner or slave' as sense 1; the citation is accurate.
'Enfranchised' as freed from prison is the primary legal sense and clearly the meaning here.

anchor_text: one which holds a trencher
summary: A 'trencher' was a flat board or plate used to serve food — held by a servant at table. 'One which holds a trencher' means a mere serving-man, a domestic servant of the lowest rank. The Old Athenian means he does not want his daughter marrying someone who is still a livery servant, waiting on others at meals.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'trencher' n. 1: 'a flat piece of wood on which meat was served or cut'; used metonymically for the office of a servant.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 137
OED s.v. 'trencher' n. 1 records the flat-board plate sense; the metonymic extension to 'office of a servant' is a standard inference from the object's use.
'Trencher' as serving-board held by a servant is the standard reading and fits the Old Athenian's social complaint precisely.

anchor_text: Three talents on the present; in future, all
summary: The Old Athenian's dowry offer is three talents immediately, with everything else after his death. Timon responds by matching the three talents ('What you bestow, in him I'll counterpoise') — providing Lucilius with enough wealth to meet the Old Athenian's standard. The scene shows Timon's generosity operating as social patronage: he personally funds a servant's marriage into a richer family.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (trans. North, 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579); monetary gifts and dowries in talents are consistent with Plutarchan Athens as Shakespeare constructs it throughout this play.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 163

Plutarch's Life of Antony is the correct broad source for the Timon material, but talent-denominated dowries are not a specific feature of the North passage cited; the citation is too loose to verify or refute the dowry-in-talents claim directly.
The scene-level gloss is accurate; Timon matching the dowry amount is exactly what the text says, and describing this as patronage funding a servant's social mobility is a fair characterization.

anchor_text: The painting is almost the natural man; For since dishonour traffics with man's nature, He is but outside
summary: Timon argues that because men are corrupted ('dishonour traffics with man's nature'), they are only their outer surfaces — which is all a painting shows. Therefore painting captures humanity just as accurately as nature does: both give you only the outside. The compliment to the Painter is also a veiled pessimism about human nature.
detail: The argument hinges on a Renaissance commonplace about the deceptiveness of appearances, but Timon pushes it further: dishonour has become so integral to human 'nature' that outwardness IS the man. The paradox anticipates Timon's later full misanthropy: if people are only their corrupt surfaces, then the play that follows is the unmasking of those surfaces. Shakespeare packs a grim philosophical claim inside what sounds like polite flattery over a painting.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'traffic' vb.: 'to deal, trade, have dealings with'; s.v. 'outside' n.: 'outward appearance, exterior.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 181
Schmidt covers 'traffic' vb. and 'outside' n. in the senses cited; the lexical support is accurate even if the interpretive claim about the passage is the annotator's own reading.

The argument that Timon equates painting's surface-rendering with humanity's reduction to corrupt exteriors is a defensible and sophisticated reading of the speech's logic; the anticipation of later misanthropy is a legitimate thematic note, not an overreach.

anchor_text: your jewel Hath suffered under praise
summary: Timon says the jewel has been harmed by being praised too much: the Jeweller's flattery has set expectations so high that the real stone cannot live up to them. The irony is characteristic of the scene — excess praise devalues rather than enhances. Timon is also, obliquely, commenting on the flattery directed at himself by everyone in the room.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'suffer' vb. 5: 'to sustain injury, be damaged.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 189
Schmidt s.v. 'suffer' vb. 5 records 'to sustain injury, be damaged' as a standard Shakespearean sense; the citation is accurate.

The reading that excessive praise sets expectations the jewel cannot meet, and that this obliquely comments on the flattery directed at Timon himself, is mainstream and clearly in the dramatic irony of the scene.

anchor_text: It would unclew me quite
summary: 'Unclew' means to unwind a ball of thread completely — to undo or ruin. Timon jokes that paying the praised-up price for the jewel would unravel him financially. The word is a comic exaggeration, but in the context of the play the joke will prove grim prophecy: Timon's prodigal spending does exactly unwind him.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'unclew' vb.: 'to unwind (a clew or ball of yarn); to undo, ruin.' The Timon passage is one of the earliest recorded uses.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 194
OED does record 'unclew' vb. as 'to unwind a clew or ball of yarn; to undo, ruin' and cites Timon among its earliest uses; the claim is accurate.
'Unclew' as unwind-a-ball-of-thread/ruin is accurate, and reading Timon's comic exaggeration as grim foreshadowing is appropriate given the play's trajectory.

anchor_text: Will you be chid?
summary: 'Chid' is the past participle of 'chide,' meaning to scold or rebuke. Timon warns the merchants and others, as Apemantus enters, that they are about to be scolded. Apemantus is the play's resident cynic who spares no one, and Timon's tone is affectionate — he is not alarmed, just amused.

sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'chide': 'to scold, rebuke, rail at.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 203
Onions s.v. 'chide' records 'to scold, rebuke, rail at' as the standard sense; the citation is accurate.
'Chid' as past participle of 'chide' (to scold) is unambiguous, and reading Timon's tone as affectionate rather than alarmed fits the dialogue.

anchor_text: Till I be gentle, stay thou for thy good morrow; When thou art Timon's dog, and these knaves honest
summary: Apemantus refuses Timon's polite greeting ('good morrow') by saying he will return it only when Timon is his dog and the flatterers are honest — that is, never. Calling himself a 'dog' is a loaded word: Apemantus is a Cynic philosopher (Greek kynikos, 'dog-like'), a school that preached disdain for wealth, social convention, and flattery. The Cynics took the dog as their symbol because, like dogs, they lived without shame and said exactly what they thought.

anchor_text: The best, for the innocence
summary: Asked how he likes the Painter's picture, Apemantus says it is 'the best, for the innocence' — meaning it is the best thing about it that it is harmless, inoffensive, merely a picture and not a real human being. 'Innocence' here means 'harmlessness' (no capacity to do evil), a backhanded compliment: Apemantus prefers the painting to the people because a painting cannot flatter, lie, or betray.

anchor_text: He wrought better that made the painter; and yet he's but a filthy piece of work
summary: Apemantus builds a syllogism: God made the painter better than the painter made the picture — but since the painter is himself 'a filthy piece of work,' even God's making doesn't amount to much. The joke demolishes both the Painter's art and the Painter as a human being in a single breath.

The syllogism structure is correctly identified: God made the painter better than the painter's product, but since the painter is contemptible, the compliment collapses — a defensible and tight reading of the joke's logic.

anchor_text: Not so well as plain dealing, which will not cost a man a doit
summary: A 'doit' was the smallest Dutch coin, worth a fraction of an English penny — proverbially the cheapest thing imaginable. Apemantus prefers honest ('plain') dealing to a costly jewel: honesty is free, the jewel is expensive, but the jewel is useless while honesty is priceless. The saying neatly inverts the marketplace values the scene has been celebrating.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'doit' n.: 'a small Dutch copper coin, worth about half an English farthing; proverbially used for an extreme trifle.' Cf. Othello 4.2: 'I would not put a doit in her purse.'

'Doit' as proverbially cheapest coin and the inversion of marketplace values (honesty is free; the jewel is costly but worthless by comparison) is a correct and mainstream reading.

anchor_text: How now, philosopher! Thou liest. Art not one? Yes. Then I lie not
summary: Apemantus and the Poet trade a staccato logical trap. Calling Apemantus a philosopher, the Poet is teasing him; Apemantus denies it ('thou liest'). But when pressed — 'Art not one?' — he admits he is. So 'then I lie not.' Apemantus then reverses the move on the Poet: a poet tells fictions, so when the Poet praised Timon in verse, he 'feigned' a worthy man — the truth is that Timon is only 'worthy' as a dupe for flatterers. The exchange dramatizes the Cynic's rejection of social polishing.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 239
Schmidt s.v. 'feign' records 'to invent, pretend, represent in fiction' as the standard sense; the citation supports the reading.
The staccato logical-trap exchange is correctly described; the move where Apemantus exploits 'feigned' to mean a poet's praise is by definition fictional is the standard reading of this dialogue.

anchor_text: 'Tis Alcibiades, and some twenty horse, All of companionship
summary: Alcibiades arrives with a military escort of twenty horsemen. In the play he is Timon's soldier-friend, drawn from Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades: a brilliant Athenian general who was repeatedly exiled by Athens and eventually marched on the city he had served. His first appearance here, welcomed by Timon, sets up a parallel story of a great man betrayed by the city that should honour him.
detail: Plutarch describes Alcibiades (c. 450–404 BC) as the ward of Pericles, an associate of Socrates, handsome and charismatic, and repeatedly undone by Athenian ingratitude. Shakespeare's Alcibiades mirrors Timon: both are ruined by Athens, both respond with violence — Timon through cursing, Alcibiades through war — but Alcibiades ultimately shows mercy where Timon does not. North's translation of Plutarch was Shakespeare's source.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades (trans. North, 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579) — the primary source for the Alcibiades material throughout the play.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 263
Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades (trans. North, 1579) is a genuine and recognised source for Shakespeare's Alcibiades material in this play, confirmed by Folger and standard source scholarship.
The Plutarchan identification of Alcibiades and the parallel-fates structure (both ruined by Athens, both respond with violence, but Alcibiades shows mercy) is standard scholarship on this play.

anchor_text: Aches contract and starve your supple joints
summary: Apemantus curses the group as they salute: may aches seize and waste ('starve') their flexible joints. In Shakespeare's English 'aches' was pronounced 'aitches' (two syllables), rhyming with 'laiches.' 'Starve' here means 'wither, waste away' rather than die of hunger. The curse is a grotesque parody of the courtly 'welcome' gestures he has just watched.

anchor_text: The strain of man's bred out Into baboon and monkey
summary: Apemantus says that humanity has degenerated ('bred out') into baboon and monkey — that the false courtesies he is watching are the behaviour of apes, not men. The image draws on the Renaissance conviction that courtly flattery was a form of aping — imitation without genuine thought. 'Strain' here means 'stock, breed, lineage' (as in a strain of plant).
detail: Apes and monkeys were Elizabethan bywords for mimicry and empty imitation; courtiers were satirized as monkeys in emblem literature and drama. Apemantus means that social ceremony has replaced genuine human virtue, so that what passes for humanity is merely animal mimicry dressed up in clothes. The line also picks up the Cynic contempt for ceremony that runs throughout Apemantus's speeches.

anchor_text: Plutus, the god of gold, Is but his steward
summary: Plutus was the classical god of wealth — from the Greek ploutos (riches). The First Lord says Timon is so rich that even the god of gold is merely Timon's household manager ('steward'). The compliment is extravagant flattery, but it also introduces the play's central motif: wealth as a kind of divinity. Timon's ruin will invert this — when his gold vanishes, his 'godhood' vanishes with it.

anchor_text: no meed but he repays Sevenfold above itself; no gift to him But breeds the giver a return exceeding All use of quittance
summary: 'Meed' means reward or gift; 'quittance' means repayment or discharge of a debt. The Second Lord says every gift Timon receives, he returns sevenfold — beyond any normal standard of repayment ('all use of quittance'). 'Use' here means customary practice or interest rate. The speech is the scene's final piece of flattery, but it is also accurate: Timon's prodigal repayments are what will bankrupt him.

anchor_text: to your free heart, I do return those talents
summary: Ventidius offers to repay the money Timon spent releasing him from debtor's prison. A 'talent' was a large ancient unit of weight used as currency — roughly equivalent to a substantial annual wage for a craftsman. Timon refuses the repayment, treating the gift as unconditional.
detail: In Athens a talent of silver weighed about 26 kilograms. On the Elizabethan stage 'talents' signalled fabulous wealth; the repayment of 'doubled' talents marks Ventidius as genuinely grateful — which sharpens the irony that he later disappears from the play without helping Timon in his ruin. The scene establishes Timon's ruling conviction (TLN 317-318) that a gift given in expectation of return is not really a gift at all.

anchor_text: none / Can truly say he gives, if he receives
summary: Timon states a paradox: a gift is only genuine if the giver expects nothing back. The logic is a sentimental foundation for his entire open-handed life — and the play will test it to destruction when every friend refuses to return the favour.
detail: The aphorism resembles Seneca's Stoic thinking on beneficence (De Beneficiis 1.1-2: a benefit freely given is its own reward; the expectation of return corrupts the act). Shakespeare is probably working from a common Renaissance commonplace rather than directly from Seneca. The line is Timon's creed in compressed form; its irony is that the whole world around him does not share it.

sources.name: Seneca

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 317

Framing the aphorism as Timon's creed — a sentimental paradox that the play tests to destruction — is a defensible mainstream reading; the Seneca parallel is noted as probable commonplace rather than direct borrowing, which is appropriately cautious.

anchor_text: faults that are rich are fair
summary: Timon wryly notes that the wealthy can get away with behaviour the poor cannot — the rich man's faults look 'fair' (fine, acceptable) because his wealth covers them. The line is slyly self-aware: he knows he is being indulgent but does it anyway.
detail: The aphorism has the ring of a proverb; compare Timon's later bitter inversion when he discovers that poverty makes his former faults unforgivable. The word 'fair' does double service: it means both 'acceptable' and 'handsome,' so the rich man's faults are literally beautified by his money. The Poet's fable of Fortune's hill in 1.1 is the play's structural version of the same idea.

anchor_text: ceremony was but devis'd at first / To set a gloss on faint deeds
summary: Timon argues that formal ceremony — bowing, elaborate courtesy — was invented only to disguise weak or hollow behaviour. 'A gloss on faint deeds' means a shine put over weak actions. He dismisses the lords' formal standing because, he claims, true friendship needs no such performance.
detail: The speech shares ground with Henry V's meditation on ceremony the night before Agincourt (Henry V 4.1): there ceremony is the 'idol' that flatters kings; here Timon turns its emptiness into a compliment (his friends' love is too real to need it). The dramatic irony is that every lord in the room is performing exactly the 'hollow welcomes' and 'recanting goodness' Timon says ceremony covers. Apemantus, watching, understands this.

anchor_text: confess'd it; hang'd it, have you not?
summary: Apemantus parodies a legal proverb: 'Confess and be hanged' — meaning once you confess a crime you are hanged for it. The lords have 'confessed' that they owe everything to Timon; Apemantus sarcastically asks why they have not been metaphorically hanged (punished, destroyed) for admitting the debt.
detail: The proverb 'confess and be hanged' was proverbial for the futility of confession — you expose yourself and gain nothing but punishment. Apemantus twists it: the lords' protestations of gratitude are their confession of debt; the play will eventually see them 'hanged' by their own ingratitude. It is Apemantus's first verbal jab, establishing him immediately as the play's discomforting truth-teller.

anchor_text: Ira furor brevis est
summary: Latin: 'Anger is a brief madness.' The line is a quotation from the Roman poet Horace (Epistles 1.2.62). Timon uses it to excuse Apemantus's permanent bad temper — but the joke is that Apemantus is never briefly angry; he is always angry, so the proverb does not apply.
detail: Horace's full line is 'Ira furor brevis est: animum rege, qui nisi paret / imperat' — 'Anger is a brief madness; govern the mind, for unless it obeys it commands.' The Epistles were a standard school text; an educated Elizabethan audience would catch the allusion and note that Timon's half-quotation omits the moral instruction ('govern the mind'), which is precisely what neither Timon nor Apemantus can do. The line foreshadows Timon's own consuming rage later in the play.

anchor_text: 't'would choke me, for I should / Ne'er flatter thee
summary: Apemantus refuses Timon's food with a dark pun: the food would choke him because eating it means accepting Timon's hospitality, which would morally require him to flatter his host — and flattery would stick in his throat before the food did.

anchor_text: dip their meat / In one man's blood; and all the madness is, / He cheers them up too
summary: Apemantus turns the feast into a sinister image: the guests 'dip their meat' in Timon's blood, meaning they eat at his cost and will eventually devour him. The image evokes Judas, who 'dipped his hand in the dish' with Jesus at the Last Supper and then betrayed him — a betrayal at the table by a trusted companion.
detail: The Geneva Bible's account of the Last Supper (Matthew 26:23) has Jesus identify his betrayer as 'he that dippeth his hand with me in the dish.' Elizabethan readers would hear the gospel echo: Timon playing Christ to his treacherous disciples. The extra sting, 'he cheers them up too,' means Timon actively toasts and encourages the men who are consuming him — the willing host of his own ruin. Apemantus, who refuses to eat at all, positions himself as the one man outside this sacrament of betrayal.

anchor_text: parts bread with him, pledges / The breath of him in a divided draught
summary: To 'part bread' and share a drink (a 'divided draught') was the ancient mark of friendship — sharing food and cup from the same loaf and vessel sealed a bond. Apemantus says the very man who does this 'is the readiest man to kill him,' meaning the closest companion is the most dangerous betrayer.
detail: Sharing bread (breaking it together) and pledging a toast from the same cup were formal acts of good faith in classical and Renaissance culture; to violate the bond of shared salt and bread (the violation of 'hospitality') was a moral outrage. Apemantus inverts the sign: intimacy of the table is precisely the access a murderer needs. The argument echoes Judas at the Last Supper, but Apemantus is speaking as a pure cynic about general human nature, not making a theological point.

Sharing bread and pledging from a shared cup as formal acts of friendship violated by betrayal is well established in classical and Renaissance culture; the gloss neither over-reads nor invents a specific allusion.

anchor_text: Honest water, which ne'er left man i' the mire
summary: Apemantus praises plain water as the only 'honest' drink because it does not intoxicate (leave a man 'in the mire,' stuck in drunken mud). Unlike wine, water flatters nobody and asks for nothing. His drinking of water at Timon's feast is a pointed refusal to participate in the feast's false sociability.
detail: The Cynic philosopher tradition — from Diogenes of Sinope onward — prized simple living, including plain water over wine, as proof that one needed nothing from the corrupt social world. Apemantus throughout the scene performs the Cynic role: refusing meat, refusing wine, offering a prayer for himself alone (TLN 370-379), and eating only 'root' (TLN 379). The word 'honest' is loaded: it means both morally trustworthy and, in the older sense, plain and undisguised — exactly what the flatterers around Timon are not.

The Cynic philosopher tradition of plain living including water over wine is directly relevant to Apemantus's established role, and the double sense of 'honest' (morally trustworthy / plain and undisguised) is a sound lexical point.

anchor_text: Immortal gods, I crave no pelf; / I pray for no man but myself
summary: Apemantus delivers his own 'grace' (the short prayer said before meals in England) but makes it a prayer for himself alone — the opposite of Christian communal grace. 'Pelf' means money or ill-gotten gains. The whole short poem (TLN 370-379) is a Cynic creed: trust nobody, need nothing, rely on no one.
detail: In Elizabethan England, grace before meals was a standard Protestant communal prayer, typically including thanks to God and a blessing on the company. Apemantus parodies the form but inverts its content — he prays selfishly, distrusts every item that communal prayer takes for granted (oaths, bonds, friends, keepers), and ends 'Rich men sin, and I eat root,' contrasting his ascetic diet with the lords' corrupt feasting. 'Pelf' specifically suggests dirty or base money, money got by cheating. The prayer doubles as a compressed statement of Apemantus's Cynical philosophy.

anchor_text: breakfast of enemies than a dinner of friends
summary: Timon jests that Alcibiades would rather have 'a breakfast of enemies' — cut-down soldiers — than a dinner of friends, because a soldier lives among the dead. Alcibiades confirms the joke ('So they were bleeding-new'). The exchange establishes Alcibiades as a warrior by nature, not a courtly flatterer — which is why he alone keeps faith with Timon in the end.
detail: The wit depends on treating 'enemies' as food: a 'breakfast' of fresh-slaughtered foes whom Alcibiades would eat with appetite. The hyperbole is affectionate, and Alcibiades's reply — 'I could wish my best friend at such a feast' — turns the joke darkly: he would happily fight even friends. Apemantus immediately seizes on this ('Would all those flatterers were thine enemies then'), showing that Alcibiades's honest violence is preferable to the flatterers' false friendship.

summary: Timon compares useless friends — those never called upon in need — to expensive musical instruments shut in their cases, never played, their music kept inside. The simile is meant as a compliment: Timon values friendship above all, and a friend never used is a gift wasted. The irony the audience feels is that the friends' 'music' — their professed love — is also locked away, unavailable when Timon will need it.

anchor_text: What means that trump
summary: A 'tucket' (as the stage direction names it) is a short fanfare of trumpet-notes, used in Elizabethan theatre to signal the approach of a noble person or procession. Here it heralds the entry of Cupid and the masquing ladies. Timon's question ('What means that trump?') is addressed to a servant — the fanfare is unannounced, part of the surprise entertainment.

anchor_text: The five best Senses / Acknowledge thee their patron
summary: Cupid enters and presents the masque in praise of Timon, saying the five senses — hearing, taste, touch, smell, and sight — all salute him as their patron, because his lavish table gratifies them all. The masque is itself an extreme symbol of Timon's extravagance: he even has the gods of love and desire perform in his honour.
detail: In classical and Renaissance iconography Cupid (Latin Amor; Greek Eros) was the god of erotic love, son of Venus — but in masque contexts he often functioned as a presenter celebrating the virtue of the host. The five-senses conceit was common in Renaissance allegory and masque: the patron whose house satisfies all the senses is the perfection of hospitality. Apemantus's response (TLN 432-445) treats the whole masque as vanity and madness — two opposed readings of the same theatrical spectacle.

anchor_text: what a sweep of vanity comes this way: / They dance! they are mad women
summary: The masque of ladies dressed as Amazons was a fashionable form of aristocratic entertainment in Shakespeare's time. Apemantus dismisses it as a 'sweep of vanity' — an ostentatious rush of empty display. Amazons were legendary warrior women from classical myth; their appearance as costumed dancers at a private feast was a courtly compliment to both the ladies and the host.
detail: Court masques, in which noble ladies disguised themselves in allegorical costumes and danced with male partners from the audience, were extremely expensive entertainments associated with Jacobean court culture (Ben Jonson and Inigo Jones produced many for the court of James I). The Amazon costume — warrior women who lived without men — was particularly common in masques, combining classical allusion with the paradox of aggressive femininity turned to graceful performance. Apemantus's contempt for the whole 'pomp' is the Cynic philosopher's standard response to excess; his 'oil and root' contrast (TLN 435) is his own ascetic diet set against the feast's extravagance.

anchor_text: for the worst is filthy; and would not hold taking, I / doubt me
summary: First Lady says Timon 'takes us even at the best'; Apemantus replies that 'the worst is filthy and would not hold taking' — meaning 'taking' in the sense of being taken sexually. He implies the ladies (dressed as warrior Amazons) are courtesans whose 'worst' uses do not bear being 'taken up' on. anchor_text: scald such chickens as you are. Would we could see you at Corinth
summary: The Fool's mistress is 'setting on water to scald such chickens as you are' — to treat you (the creditors' servants) like plucked birds fit only for the pot. 'Corinth' is the key: in Elizabethan slang, 'a merry Greek' or a visit to 'Corinth' meant a brothel or a courtesan's house, because the ancient city of Corinth was famous for sacred prostitution at the temple of Aphrodite. The Fool is simultaneously inviting the servants to visit his mistress and calling them fit only to be her clients.
detail: Corinth's reputation for prostitution was ancient: Strabo (Geography 8.6.20) reports that the temple of Aphrodite there kept more than a thousand sacred prostitutes. This gave rise to the proverb 'Not every man's lot to go to Corinth' (not everyone can afford it). In Elizabethan slang, 'a Corinthian' was a merry companion fond of wenching; Thomas Dekker and others use 'Corinth' explicitly for brothels. anchor_text: I think no usurer but has a fool to his servant

anchor_text: like a philosopher, with two stones more than's artificial one

The pun knits the scene's two themes — usury and lechery — into one joke.

anchor_text: hard fractions, With certain half-caps and cold-moving nods, They froze me into silence

anchor_text: Their blood is cak'd, 'tis cold, it seldom flows; 'Tis lack of kindly warmth they are not kind
summary: Timon offers a comic-pathetic physiological excuse for the senators' ingratitude: old men's blood runs thick and cold, so they cannot be 'kind' — and 'kind' puns on both 'generous' and 'according to their natural kind' (i.e., their nature as fellow humans). The wordplay turns a failure of generosity into a medical condition, and Timon's speech excuses the senators to avoid facing the truth about their deliberate rejection.

Timon unconsciously continues the excuse-making that has characterized his entire relationship with money, substituting physiology for moral judgment.

anchor_text: That thought is bounty's foe; Being free itself, it thinks all others so
summary: Flavius's closing couplet is the scene's final epigram: the thought that Timon's fortunes can fall among his friends ('That thought is bounty's foe') is bounty's enemy, because a truly generous nature, being itself free and open-handed ('free' means liberal, unbounded), naturally assumes that all others are the same — and is therefore blind to the calculating self-interest of those around it. Flavius closes the scene not with blame but with a kind of tragic sympathy: Timon is ruined by the very quality that made him lovable.
detail: The rhyming couplet (foe / so) signals the scene's formal close and the summary judgment on Timon's character. 'Free' in Elizabethan usage was the highest compliment for a generous person — lavish, open-handed, uncalculating. The irony is that Timon's 'free' nature is simultaneously his greatest virtue and the mechanism of his destruction: he cannot conceive of ingratitude because he has never felt it. The same paradox — bounty as vulnerability — drives the whole play's de casibus arc.

anchor_text: friendship such a faint and milky heart
summary: 'Milky' here means weak, pale, and bloodless — the opposite of the hot red blood associated with courage and loyalty. A 'milky heart' is a cowardly, watery one. Flaminius is asking: has friendship become so thin and spineless that it curdles in less than two nights?
detail: The usage connects to the frequent Shakespearean metaphor contrasting 'milk' (whiteness, timidity, sentimentality) with 'blood' (passion, courage, loyalty). Compare Macbeth's 'too full o' the milk of human kindness' (1.5) and Lady Macbeth's call to 'unsex me here' and fill her with 'direst cruelty.' Here the meaning is specifically that Lucullus's friendship has no substance — it 'turns' (curdles, like milk) the moment money is needed. 'In less than two nights' suggests the speed of the betrayal has shocked Flaminius as much as the betrayal itself.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'milky' adj., sense 2: 'Resembling milk in character; weak, effeminate, timid, mild.' (OED Online, 2nd ed.)

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'milky': 'tame, feeble, cowardly.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 892

OED s.v. 'milky' adj. sense 2 ('weak, effeminate, timid') and Onions ('tame, feeble, cowardly') are real and accurate sources that directly support the annotation's reading of 'milky heart' as weak and bloodless.

'Milky' as weak, pale, and bloodless — the antithesis of the hot-blooded courage associated with loyalty — is the established Shakespearean usage, and the Macbeth parallel ('too full o' the milk of human kindness') confirms the idiom; the reading that Lucullus's friendship 'turns' (curdles like milk) the moment money is needed is fully supported by the scene.

anchor_text: borrow so many talents
summary: A talent was the largest unit of currency in the ancient Greek world — roughly 6,000 silver drachmas, about 26 kg of silver, and many years' wages for a laborer. 'So many talents' (the amount left unspecified) is what one of Timon's men begged of Lucullus and was refused, and what Servilius now requests of Lucius. Lucius then waves the request off with an absurd flourish — Timon 'cannot want fifty-five hundred talents' (TLN 935), his own wild overestimate of Timon's wealth — and so finds a pretext to deny the far smaller sum actually needed.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'talent' n., sense 1a: 'A denomination of weight and of money used by the ancient Greeks, Romans, and other peoples, varying considerably at different periods and in different countries' (the Attic talent = 6,000 drachmas).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 910

OED talent sense 1a is a real entry with the quoted definition; the Attic talent weighing ~26 kg (~57 lb) equal to 6,000 drachmas is accurate; North's 1579 translation uses 'talent' throughout as standard Athenian currency denomination, making the citation supportive even though the specific locus is the Life of Antony rather than a dedicated Life of Timon.

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Trimmed the summary's conflation: 5,500 talents is Lucius's sarcastic overestimate of Timon's wealth (TLN 935), not a borrowing request, and Servilius's request leaves the sum unspecified; OED (source-verified) is kept.

detail: The talent's vast scale measures both Timon's reputed riches and the meanness of the friends who will not lend.

anchor_text: disfurnish myself against such a good time
summary: 'Disfurnish' means to strip or deprive oneself of resources — to spend or commit money so that one is left without. Lucius claims he was foolish to have laid out all his cash right before this moment when Timon needed him, so he has 'purchased the day before for a little part' (spent on a trifle) and thereby 'undo[ne] a great deal of honour' — wrecked his chance to look generous. The word is standard Elizabethan business vocabulary.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'disfurnish': 'to deprive of furniture, equipment, or means; to strip.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'disfurnish' v.: 'To deprive of furniture or equipment; to strip of resources.' Earliest citation 1568.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 941

OED does carry 'disfurnish' v. with the sense 'deprive of furniture or equipment; strip of resources'; Collins records earliest use c. 1525–35 (not 1568 as claimed, but the word is genuine and the definition accurate); Schmidt's definition 'to deprive of furniture, equipment, or means; to strip' matches standard references.

The gloss accurately captures 'disfurnish' as stripping oneself of resources and correctly explains that Lucius is blaming a recent expenditure as the excuse for his refusal — the reading is mainstream and supported by the surrounding dialogue.

anchor_text: this is the world's soul; and just of the same piece Is every flatterer's spirit
summary: The First Stranger says that what they have just watched — a man lavishly professing love to Timon, then refusing him the moment he is asked for anything — is the essential nature ('soul') of how the world works. 'Just of the same piece' means made of the same cloth, the same substance. The image turns a private act of hypocrisy into a specimen of universal moral fabric.
detail: The Strangers function as a choric device throughout Act 3: they have no personal stake in Timon's fall, which makes their moral commentary authoritative in a way that the self-interested lords' words are not. The First Stranger's analysis — that a flatterer who 'dips in the same dish' is actually no friend at all — picks up the ancient table-fellowship test (sharing a meal signals alliance), and his conclusion, 'policy sits above conscience' (line 984), is one of the play's bleakest thematic formulations.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'piece': 'stuff, material, fabric; of the same piece = of the same nature.'

sources.name: Jowett, Timon of Athens (Oxford, 2004)
sources.citation: Jowett, John, ed. Timon of Athens, Oxford Shakespeare (2004), note to 3.2.60–61: the Strangers as the play's moral chorus, introduced to provide disinterested judgement.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 960

Jowett's 2004 Oxford Shakespeare edition is real and search results confirm it discusses the Strangers in 3.2 as choric figures offering disinterested moral judgement; Schmidt's 'piece' as 'stuff, material, fabric' is standard lexicographic sense; the specific note attribution is consistent with the edition's editorial approach.
The Strangers-as-moral-chorus reading is well-established in the critical tradition, 'just of the same piece' as 'made of the same cloth' is the standard gloss, and the annotation does not overreach.

anchor_text: dips in the same dish? for, in My knowing, Timon has been this lord's father
summary: To 'dip in the same dish' means to eat from the same bowl — a sign of intimate friendship. The phrase echoes the Last Supper, where Jesus identifies his betrayer as the one who 'dippeth his hand with me in the dish' (Matthew 26:23). Shakespeare's audience would hear the Judas allusion instantly: Lucius is a dinner-guest of Timon's who has now betrayed him, just as Judas was a companion at table who handed Jesus over.
detail: The table-fellowship betrayal is one of the play's governing images. Timon's great banquets in Acts 1–2 were the site of his generosity and the proof of his 'friends'; Act 3's cascade of refusals turns every guest into a Judas-figure. The First Stranger drives the point home by noting that Timon had been 'this lord's father' — not just a friend but a patron-parent who 'kept his credit with his purse' and 'paid his men their wages,' making the betrayal still more intimate and the parallel to Judas more pointed.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 26:23 (Geneva 1599): 'He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, he shall betray me.' Compare Mark 14:20.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 962

Matthew 26:23 in the 1599 Geneva Bible reads exactly 'He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, he shall betray me' — the citation is accurate word for word, and the Judas-betrayal identification is the verse's explicit subject.

The biblical parallel to Matthew 26:23 is defensible — 'dip in the same dish' is the Gospel phrase for Judas's betrayal and the connection to table-fellowship betrayal is a mainstream reading for this play, though the allusion is probable rather than certain.

anchor_text: He ne'er drinks But Timon's silver treads upon his lip
summary: The First Stranger is saying that every time Lucius lifts a cup to drink, he is drinking from silver plate bought with Timon's money. 'Timon's silver treads upon his lip' is a compressed metaphor: the cup touches the lip, but it is Timon's generosity — in the literal form of silverware — that actually makes contact. It is a devastating image of ingratitude made concrete: even the metal against Lucius's mouth is borrowed.
detail: The series of images the First Stranger builds here — Timon as father (line 963), Timon's money paying the servants' wages (lines 965–966), Timon's silver on his lip (lines 966–967) — amounts to a list of the ways in which Lucius's entire material existence was funded by the man he just refused. The rhetorical figure is a kind of synecdoche: the silver cup stands for the whole system of Timon's bounty now turned to ash.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'tread': 'to press, to come into contact with'; the usage here is a compressed catachresis noted by most editors.

sources.name: Jowett, Timon of Athens (Oxford, 2004)
sources.citation: Jowett, John, ed. Timon of Athens, Oxford Shakespeare (2004), note to 3.2.66–67: the silver-on-the-lip image as the culminating specimen of Timon's absorbed generosity.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 966

Jowett's 2004 Oxford edition is genuine and discusses the silver imagery in 3.2, but the specific note attributed to lines '3.2.66–67' with the quoted wording 'culminating specimen of Timon's absorbed generosity' cannot be independently verified; Schmidt's 'tread' entry in the Perseus-hosted Lexicon could not be retrieved to confirm the exact phrasing 'to press, to come into contact with'.

The reading that 'Timon's silver' refers literally to silverware given by Timon and now touching Lucius's lip is the most natural and editorially standard interpretation; calling the figure synecdoche is appropriate and the annotation does not overreach.

anchor_text: I never tasted Timon in my life, Nor came any of his bounties over me
summary: 'Tasted Timon' means experienced or benefited from Timon's generosity — 'taste' here carries the sense of 'have a share of, partake of.' The First Stranger is saying he has never eaten at Timon's table or received a gift from him, making his moral outrage all the more striking: he is defending a man he has never personally profited from, purely on the grounds of decency.
detail: The verb 'taste' meaning 'to experience or enjoy a share of something' is standard Elizabethan usage (OED 'taste' v. sense 7). The line is thematically important: the First Stranger's willingness to champion Timon without personal benefit makes him the play's most credible moral witness, by contrast to Lucius, who has 'tasted' Timon in every sense and still refuses him. The same logic governs the Strangers' role throughout 3.2.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'taste' v., sense 7: 'To have experience of, to partake of, to enjoy or undergo (something); to have a share in.' Cited from 16th and 17th century texts.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 974

OED does record 'taste' v. in the experiential/partaking sense with citations from the 16th and 17th centuries; the etymological record confirms 'have experience of' from at least early 14th century, making this a well-attested and correctly characterised sense.
'Taste' meaning 'partake of, have experience of' is standard Elizabethan usage and the annotation's reading of the First Stranger as an impartial moral witness is the mainstream critical view.

anchor_text: Men must learn now with pity to dispense; For policy sits above conscience
summary: 'Policy' in Shakespeare's English means calculating self-interest, political cunning — the pursuit of personal advantage regardless of moral principle. 'Conscience' is the internal moral sense. The First Stranger ends the scene with a bitter aphorism: the world has been so thoroughly reshaped by cynical self-interest that even pity must be 'dispensed with' (given out sparingly, withheld at will), because shrewd calculation now ranks above moral feeling. It is the play's bleakest one-line summary of what Athens has become.
detail: The word 'policy' carried in Shakespeare a specific and pejorative charge: it evoked Machiavellian statecraft, the idea that a ruler (or a man of the world) must deceive, manipulate, and suppress sentiment in favour of cold strategy. Characters described as 'politic' are calculating hypocrites. The line generalizes from Lucius's refusal just witnessed: in a world where policy governs, a man of open generosity like Timon is not merely naive but structurally exposed. The Strangers exit on this note, leaving the theatre audience as the only witnesses left.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'policy': '(with derogatory implication) cunning, artful scheming; worldly wisdom; expedient conduct as opposed to principle.'

sources.name: Jowett, Timon of Athens (Oxford, 2004)
sources.citation: Jowett, John, ed. Timon of Athens, Oxford Shakespeare (2004), note to 3.2.83-84: the closing couplet as the scene's choric verdict on Athenian moral collapse.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 983

anchor_text: touch'd and found base metal
summary: To 'touch' a metal meant to test its purity by rubbing it against a touchstone — a piece of dark stone used by assayers to judge whether gold or silver was genuine. A metal that proved 'base' (i.e. debased alloy rather than pure gold) was worthless. The servant is saying all three lords who received Timon's generosity have been tested and shown to be counterfeit friends.
detail: Touchstone assaying was familiar Elizabethan commercial practice: goldsmiths carried touchstones to verify coinage. Shakespeare uses the image repeatedly as a metaphor for testing true character against false (cf. As You Like It, where the Fool is named Touchstone). Here the servant's image is precise and bitter: Timon's bounty was gold; his friends are brass.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'touch' v. sense 15a: 'To test (gold or silver) with a touchstone; to assay'; and s.v. 'base' adj. sense 5: 'Of metal: not pure; alloyed with a baser metal; hence, of inferior quality.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 991
OED s.v. 'touch' v. (assay sense) and s.v. 'base' adj. (debased-metal sense) are both real, well-documented OED entries that directly support the touchstone-testing metaphor described.

Touchstone assaying as a metaphor for testing character is standard Elizabethan usage and the servant's application — Timon's bounty as gold, the lords as base alloy — follows directly and precisely from the line.

anchor_text: His friends, like physicians, / Thrice give him over
summary: To 'give over' a patient meant for a physician to declare the case hopeless and withdraw from treatment — to pronounce the patient as good as dead. Sempronius says that since three lords (Lucius, Lucullus, Ventidius) have already 'given him over,' he should not be obliged to step in as a fourth. The conceit is thoroughly self-serving: he casts ingratitude as medical protocol.
detail: The number three is pointed: early modern medicine, following classical humoral theory, often required consultation among several physicians before pronouncing a case terminal. The irony is savage — Timon's 'disease' is poverty, curable by any one of them; their collective refusal is pure choice dressed up as professional consensus. Sempronius's logic is that Timon has already been condemned by a quorum, so his own cruelty is merely redundant.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'give over' phrase 4b: 'To abandon (a patient) as incurable, to cease attending or treating.' First citation 1576.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'give over': 'to leave off, to abandon a hopeless cause or case.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 997

OED s.v. 'give over' (abandon a patient as incurable) is a genuine phrasal-verb sense with early-modern citations, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon covers this phrase; both sources support the summary.

'Give over' as abandoning a hopeless patient is well-attested; the link between 'thrice' and the three named lords is explicit in the text, and the self-serving irony reading is fully supported by Sempronius's own words.

anchor_text: The devil knew not what he did when he made man politic; he crossed himself by't
summary: 'Politic' means cunning, scheming, self-serving — a common Elizabethan negative. 'Crossed himself' carries a double meaning: (1) the devil made a mistake ('crossed' = thwarted his own purposes) because a man skilled at self-serving deceit now competes with the devil at his own trade; and (2) 'crossed himself' means to make the sign of the cross — an ironic image of the devil accidentally performing a Christian gesture. The servant is saying that human political cunning surpasses even the devil's evil.
detail: The theological joke was a commonplace in satirical contexts: the devil, inventor of sin, has been out-sinned by man. The second meaning — the devil crossing himself in horror at man's wickedness, performing a pious act by accident — sharply reverses normal expectation (the cross protects against the devil; here the devil uses it as a reflex of shock). The speech signals the servant as a choric moraliser, drawing out the scene's satiric logic.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'politic': 'scheming, crafty, self-interested.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cross' v. sense 4a: 'To thwart, to frustrate'; and s.v. 'cross oneself': 'to make the sign of the cross.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1013

Onions s.v. 'politic' (scheming, crafty) is a standard Elizabethan pejorative sense, and OED s.v. 'cross' v. (thwart/frustrate) plus the reflexive 'cross oneself' (sign of the cross) are both real and distinct OED senses supporting the double-meaning reading.

Both senses of 'crossed himself' — thwarted his own purpose and made the sign of the cross — are mainstream editorial readings, and the theological jest (human cunning out-sinning the devil) is a genuine Elizabethan satirical commonplace, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: Doors, that were ne'er acquainted with their wards / Many a bounteous year, must be employ'd
summary: 'Wards' are the ridges inside a lock that a key must fit — the working parts of a door's lock mechanism. Doors that were 'never acquainted with their wards' for 'many a bounteous year' means: during Timon's open-handed prosperity his doors stood perpetually open and the locks were never used. Now those same doors must be locked and kept shut against creditors. The closing couplet plays on 'keep his house' — meaning both 'maintain a household' and the contemporary idiom for hiding indoors to dodge debt-collectors (a debtor who 'kept house' stayed inside to avoid arrest).
detail: The legal background: in early modern England, creditors could not arrest a debtor inside his own home — only on the street or in a church porch. So 'keeping house' (remaining indoors) was a recognised debtor's tactic, and 'to keep one's house' was a recognized phrase for such concealment. The servant's final couplet thus compresses Timon's fall into a single bitter paradox: the man whose house was always open for guests must now seal it shut to keep himself safe from those same guests' claims on him.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ward' n. sense 7: 'A notch or ridge in a key or lock which prevents the turning of any key not having a corresponding notch.' And s.v. 'keep house' phrase 1b: 'to remain indoors, esp. to avoid creditors or arrest.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'keep house': 'to remain within doors (as a debtor, to avoid arrest).'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1022

OED 'ward' n. in the lock-mechanism sense and 'keep house' as a debtor's tactic of remaining indoors to avoid arrest are both well-attested in early modern legal and lexicographical sources, and Onions corroborates the idiom; the 1542 statute confirms the 'keep house' meaning in law.

The gloss on 'wards' is technically correct, the open-door-to-locked-door paradox is directly supported by the text, and 'keep house' as a debtor's legal tactic (avoiding street arrest) is well-documented early modern practice.

anchor_text: Labouring for nine
summary: 'Labouring for nine' means the hour is struggling toward nine — it is nearly, but not quite, nine in the morning. The creditors have been waiting since before the household officially opened its doors.
detail: The idiom treats the clock as straining to reach the next hour, like a labourer not yet at his destination. It signals that the servants have arrived early to be first in the queue — and still Timon has not appeared, which Philotus finds remarkable.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'labour' v. sense 4a: 'to strive, struggle, or work hard toward a point or end'; the clock-time usage is consistent with Elizabethan idiom for a moment approaching a fixed hour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1037

OED 'labour' v. is a real source, but the specific sense number 4a and the claim of a documented 'clock-time usage' for a clock straining toward a fixed hour cannot be confirmed; the annotation over-reads the OED entry as endorsing a specialised idiom that is more likely editorial inference from context.

The clock-as-labourer idiom for 'approaching but not yet at the hour' is well-attested Elizabethan usage, and the scene's conversational context (creditors marking the early hour) supports the reading exactly.

anchor_text: he was wont to shine at seven
summary: Philotus compares Timon to the sun — he used to 'shine' (hold court, be visible and generous) by seven in the morning. Lucius' Servant then extends the metaphor: a spendthrift's course is 'like the sun's' in that it rises and falls, but unlike the sun it cannot recover and rise again the next day.
detail: The sun metaphor is carefully developed across four lines: the sun's course as a figure for a great man's rise and fall is a standard Renaissance emblem. The crucial turn is 'but not, like his, recoverable' — Fortune's hill can be descended but the prodigal cannot cycle back to the top as the sun cycles back to dawn. The metaphor prepares the audience thematically for a man in irreversible decline. It also quietly echoes the play's opening Poet-figure, whose allegory of Fortune's hill (1.1) described exactly this trajectory.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'course' (the circuit of the sun as a figure for a man's life-span and fortune); the sun-as-great-man metaphor is recurrent in Shakespeare (cf. 1 Henry IV 1.2, Richard II 3.2).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1041

Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real standard reference; the sun-as-great-man metaphor and 'course' as a life-circuit are well-documented there, and the cross-references to 1H4 1.2 and R2 3.2 are genuine Shakespearean parallels.

The sun-as-great-man / Fortune's-hill trajectory is mainstream Renaissance emblem thinking, the text itself develops the metaphor across four lines with explicit comparative language ('like the sun's, but not, like his, recoverable'), and the back-reference to the Poet's opening allegory is a defensible structural observation rather than an over-reading.

anchor_text: deepest winter in Lord Timon's purse
summary: Lucius' Servant uses a seasonal metaphor: 'deepest winter' in Timon's purse means it is at its barest — a purse in midwinter, like the earth, has nothing growing or available in it. He then sharpens it: you can reach deep into it and still find nothing.
detail: The vehicle of the conceit is winter barrenness — the season when fields yield nothing. The tenor is absolute financial ruin: the purse is not merely low but empty, no matter how far you reach. This is the scene's most economical statement of Timon's bankruptcy, and it comes from a minor creditor's servant, not from Timon or Flavius — a sign that the ruin is public knowledge even among outsiders. The chill imagery continues the sun-going-down metaphor from the lines just above.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'winter' (seasonal want as a figure for poverty); compare the 'winter of our discontent' usage (Richard III 1.1) and the seasonal-poverty metaphor in As You Like It 2.1.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1046
Schmidt s.v. 'winter' for seasonal want as poverty is a real and supportable entry; the Richard III 'winter of our discontent' and As You Like It seasonal-poverty parallels are genuine.

Winter-as-barrenness / poverty is a standard Elizabethan semantic and the text itself glosses the metaphor ('that is, one may reach deep enough, and yet find little'), so the interpretation requires no stretching.

anchor_text: preferr'd you not your sums and bills
summary: A 'bill' is a written demand for repayment of a debt — what we would call an invoice or a promissory note. Flavius angrily asks why the creditors did not submit these written demands while their masters were still feasting at Timon's table and enjoying his generosity.
detail: In Elizabethan commercial practice a 'bill' was a formal written instrument recording a debt owed and a demand for payment; 'sums' are the amounts. To 'prefer' a bill is to submit or present it formally. Flavius's point is bitter: the creditors' masters ate Timon's food and accepted his presents ('smile and fawn upon his debts') — pocketing the interest on loans, implied by 'take down the interest into their gluttonous maws' — but never pressed for repayment while the benefiting was good. They now come like creditors after the feast is over.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (rev. R. D. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'bill' (a written statement of money owed; a bond or promissory note); s.v. 'prefer' (to present, submit).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1083
Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (rev. Eagleson, 1986) s.v. 'bill' and 'prefer' are real entries with accurate definitions for a written debt instrument and the act of presenting it formally.

The commercial-legal sense of 'bill' (written debt instrument) and 'prefer' (to present formally) are uncontroversial Elizabethan usage, and the gloss accurately captures Flavius's rebuke that the creditors' masters feasted without pressing their claims.

anchor_text: smile and fawn upon his debts, And take down the interest into their gluttonous maws
summary: Flavius accuses the creditors' masters of two hypocrisies at once: they smiled and flattered Timon ('fawned') while he was in debt to them, and meanwhile quietly pocketed the interest on what he owed, swallowing it ('maws' = gullets, stomachs) without complaint. The phrase combines ingratitude with greed into a single image of predatory smiling.
detail: A 'maw' is a stomach or gullet, especially of a beast or bird of prey; 'gluttonous' reinforces the animal imagery. The creditors are figured as creatures who smile and fawn (like dogs flattering their master) but who are simultaneously feeding — eating Timon's meat at his table while digesting his debt-interest. Flavius, the one honest man in the scene, is the only character who names this hypocrisy plainly. The passage is a compressed emblem of the play's central theme: the social rituals of gift and feast that mask appetite.

anchor_text: his cashiered worship
summary: 'Cashiered' means dismissed from service — Flavius has been discharged as Timon's steward because there is no household left to manage. 'His worship' was a standard form of address for a gentleman, alderman, or officer; Varro's Servant uses it mockingly — the grand title clashes with a man who is now poor and muffled in a cloak to avoid being seen. The sarcasm signals the social world's reversal: even Timon's most faithful servant is now beneath contempt to these dunning underlings.

anchor_text: Who can speak broader than he that has no house to put his head in? such may rail against great buildings
summary: Second Varro's Servant says that a man who has lost everything is free to speak as broadly (as openly, as frankly) as he likes, because he has nothing left to lose. The penniless can afford to curse great buildings — rich men's houses — because they no longer own property those buildings could threaten or take from them. Poverty grants a bitter kind of freedom of speech.

'Broader' means with greater freedom and licence, without the restraint that the propertied must exercise. The observation is cynical rather than sympathetic — Varro's Servant is not praising Flavius but dismissing his complaints as the harmless noise of the powerless.

anchor_text: His comfortable temper has forsook him
summary: 'Comfortable temper' means his habitual ease of mind and generosity of spirit — the mental disposition that made him hospitable and cheerful. 'Forsook him' means has abandoned him. Servilius is saying that Timon's characteristic good nature is gone.
detail: 'Comfortable' in Elizabethan usage means imparting or feeling comfort; it describes a disposition that gives ease and warmth to others, not merely one's own personal comfort. 'Temper' is the habitual balance of the mind and humours — not anger, but the whole cast of a person's character. The phrase is Servilius's gentle way of telling the creditors that Timon is in a mental crisis, not merely unwell in body, without directly saying he is enraged or despairing.

anchor_text: he should the sooner pay his debts, And make a clear way to the gods

anchor_text: Knock me down with 'em: cleave me to the girdle
summary: Timon responds to the flood of bills with grotesque hyperbole: knock me down with the papers, split me in half with them down to the belt ('girdle'). His violence of imagery is the sign of a mind breaking under the weight of creditors — he is not literally asking to be killed, but the language of physical ruin mirrors the financial ruin he cannot otherwise express.

The bills become weapons, and the debt becomes a literal bodily wound. This hyperbolic identification of money-debts with bodily dissolution is the rhetorical hinge from the social Timon to the wilderness Timon of Acts 4-5.

anchor_text: throw their caps at their money
summary: 'Throw their caps at' something means to give it up as hopeless — the way a man throws his cap in the air and walks away from a lost cause. anchor_text: bid all my friends again: Lucius, Lucullus, and Sempronius; all: I'll once more feast the rascals
summary: Timon abruptly decides to invite the same friends who refused him loans to a great dinner. Flavius warns there is barely enough left for 'a moderate table.' The audience, who has seen those friends deny Timon in the three preceding scenes, understands this is not a reconciliation: the feast will be a trap. Timon adds 'my cook and I'll provide,' suggesting he has something specific in mind.

The invitation scene here is theatrically important because Timon's plan is not revealed until the mock-feast itself; the audience is left to wonder whether he is truly distracted (as Flavius fears) or plotting a revenge. His insistence — 'Be it not in thy care: go' — against Flavius's financial protests signals that this feast is outside normal reckoning, fuelled not by money but by something else entirely.

anchor_text: Nothing emboldens sin so much as mercy
summary: The First Senator's opening maxim — that mercy only encourages wrongdoing — is a sententious axiom (a compact moral saying), here used to justify condemning Alcibiades's soldier without appeal. Shakespeare and Middleton deploy it as evidence of the Senate's hard-line legal philosophy, which the scene then puts under pressure.

The irony is structural: the senate that prides itself on strict law will be shown, by the end of the play, to be corrupt with usury and personal interest (see TLN 1255-1266). The senator's maxim sounds principled but is immediately enlisted to refuse even a hearing.
