anchor_text: pity is the virtue of the law, And none but tyrants use it cruelly
summary: Alcibiades argues that the law's proper virtue is pity (mercy), not severity, and that only tyrants wield the law cruelly. The line directly reverses the senator's opening maxim, setting up a debate between strict legalism and equity that runs through the whole scene.

Alcibiades is essentially making the same case Portia makes in The Merchant of Venice ('the quality of mercy is not strained,' 4.1) — that the spirit of justice requires mercy. The play is written with Middleton, and this scene is generally attributed to Shakespeare.

anchor_text: You undergo too strict a paradox, Striving to make an ugly deed look fair
summary: 'Paradox' here does not mean a logical puzzle; it means a position contrary to received opinion — a claim so against the accepted view that maintaining it is itself a kind of strain. anchor_text: his service done At Lacedaemon and Byzantium
summary: Lacedaemon is the ancient Greek name for Sparta, Athens's great rival; Byzantium is the city at the mouth of the Black Sea (modern Istanbul). Both were arenas of Athenian military operations during the Peloponnesian War period. Alcibiades argues that the condemned soldier's battlefield service at these distant, dangerous postings should outweigh a single violent crime.

The play's Alcibiades is a composite of the historical figure's repeated banishments and returns. Mentioning Lacedaemon and Byzantium is also a way of signalling that the condemned man is a veteran campaigner, not a mere civilian brawler.

anchor_text: your reverend ages love Security, I'll pawn my victories
summary: 'Security' is a financial-legal term for a pledge or guarantee against a loan or obligation. Alcibiades is ironically flattering the senators — men who love financial security — by offering to pawn (pledge) his own military victories and honour as collateral for his friend's good conduct. The financial language is pointed: in a play saturated with debt and usury, the general is forced to speak to the Senate in the only currency they understand.

Alcibiades treats his battlefield honours as a tradeable asset. This connects to the play's larger critique of Athenian society as reducible to money and usury.

anchor_text: Banish your dotage; banish usury, That makes the Senate ugly
summary: Alcibiades responds to the Senate's banishment by turning the word back on them: they should banish their own senility ('dotage') and their practice of usury (money-lending at interest). Usury was a sharp political charge in Elizabethan England as well as in classical Athens: lending money for profit was widely condemned as morally corrupt.
detail: In early modern England the legal ceiling on interest rates was set at 10% by the Statute of Usury (1571), and the moral debate about whether any interest-taking was sinful was ongoing throughout Shakespeare's career. The accusation that the senators are usurers — not just law-givers but money-lenders who have profited from Timon's debts — connects the Senate's legal cruelty to the play's economic theme. 'Dotage' (senility) adds a second accusation: the senators are both corrupt and old-and-foolish, unfit to judge a soldier in his prime. Alcibiades's lines directly anticipate his later speech (TLN 1262-1267) in which he confirms they have been lending out money at interest while he kept their enemies at bay.

anchor_text: I have kept back their foes, While they have told their money and let out Their coin upon large interest
summary: Alcibiades's closing soliloquy names the senators' real occupation: 'told their money' means counted out coins; 'let out their coin upon large interest' means lent it at high rates for profit. The parallel is exact — while he bled for Athens on the battlefield, the senators stayed safe at home and grew rich from usury. This charges the city's ruling class with a double crime: cowardice and financial exploitation.
detail: The phrase 'told their money' (counted, tallied) was the standard idiom for a miser's private auditing of his hoard. 'Let out upon large interest' is the precise language of bond-lending. That the senators are revealed as usurers — men who profit from others' debt rather than risk their own lives — connects this scene to Timon's own fate: he was ruined in part because the city's economic order runs on exploitation. Alcibiades's formulation ('I am worse than mad') registers that the injustice is of a scale that exceeds ordinary anger, mirroring Timon's own eventual excess.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'tell': 'to count, reckon.' OED s.v. 'let out,' v., phrase 6a: 'to lend (money) at interest.' For the broader usury critique, see Thomas Wilson, A Discourse upon Usury (1572), ed. Tawney (1925).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1262
Onions s.v. 'tell,' OED 'let out' phrase 6a, and Thomas Wilson's A Discourse upon Usury (1572) edited by Tawney (1925) are all confirmed real sources that support the annotation.
'Told their money' meaning counted coins and 'let out upon large interest' as bond-lending are the correct senses, and the soldier-versus-moneylender contrast is explicitly drawn in the text itself.

anchor_text: Is this the balsam that the usuring senate Pours into captains' wounds?
summary: 'Balsam' (also spelled 'balm') is a healing ointment — here the metaphorical reward that a grateful city should pour into the wounds its soldiers suffer on its behalf. Alcibiades asks: is banishment really the salve Athens gives to its defenders? The rhetorical question turns the word 'usuring' (lending at interest, exploitative) into a permanent epithet for the Senate.
detail: The word 'usuring' as an adjective applied to the Senate is Shakespeare's coinage (no other contemporary source uses 'usuring senate'). It brands the senators permanently as money-lenders rather than civic fathers. 'Balsam' for the just reward of military service had a natural audience resonance: Elizabethan soldiers who returned from Ireland or the Low Countries routinely complained of being left unpaid and neglected. The image of wounds requiring balsam also prepares for Alcibiades's final line comparing soldiers to gods ('brook as little wrongs as gods').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'balsam,' n., sense 1: 'a fragrant oleoresinous substance used as an unguent or in medicine; figuratively, a healing or soothing influence.' OED s.v. 'usuring,' adj.: 'Pertaining to or practicing usury' — the earliest adjectival usage cited is this passage.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1266

OED 'balsam' sense 1 and 'usuring' adj. are real and supportive; the claim that this passage is the earliest adjectival citation is consistent with the OED's practice of citing Shakespeare for neologisms.

The figurative sense of 'balsam' as healing reward for wounds is the plain metaphor, and 'usuring' as an adjectival coinage is supported by OED; the claim about Elizabethan soldiers' grievances is contextually plausible though not directly required by the text.

anchor_text: Soldiers should brook as little wrongs as gods
summary: 'Brook' means endure or tolerate — Alcibiades is saying soldiers should put up with insults as rarely as the gods do: that is, not at all. The gods of classical mythology were famously swift to punish those who wronged them. The comparison lifts soldiers onto a divine level of honour-sensitivity, crowning Alcibiades's argument for retaliatory violence and implicitly justifying his coming war on Athens.
detail: The sententia is a compressed version of the whole scene's debate. Alcibiades has spent the scene arguing against the Stoic senators that bearing wrongs is not true valour; this closing line gives that argument its most extreme form. The comparison of soldiers to gods in their intolerance for injury is also dangerous: it places martial honour above civic law, which is precisely what the Senate has condemned. The audience may notice that Alcibiades is about to become, in effect, a god of vengeance to Athens — as Timon had been a god of bounty.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'brook': 'to endure, tolerate, put up with.' The gods' swift punishment of those who offend them is a commonplace from Homer, Iliad 1 (Apollo's plague on the Greeks) onwards.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 1.9–52 (Apollo unleashes plague on the Greek camp; the gods do not tolerate injury to their honor). The idea is a stock element of Greek theogony underlying both epic and tragic tradition.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1273

Onions s.v. 'brook' is a standard real reference, and Iliad 1.9–52 does depict Apollo unleashing plague because Agamemnon dishonoured his priest — a genuine example of divine intolerance of injury to their honour.

The gloss on 'brook' as endure is correct, and reading the gods-comparison as Alcibiades crowning his anti-Stoic argument and prefiguring his role as instrument of divine vengeance is a defensible and mainstream interpretation.

anchor_text: swallow follows not summer more willing
summary: Second Lord flatters Timon with a comparison: just as the swallow follows summer wherever it goes, so the lords follow him. Timon's immediate aside (TLN 1297-98) turns the compliment against the speaker: like the swallow, these 'summer-birds' follow the warmth of his money and will be just as quick to leave it. The simile sets up the whole scene's exposure of fair-weather friendship.

sources.name: Aesop / proverbial
sources.citation: The swallow as the type of the fair-weather companion who comes with summer and vanishes with the cold is an ancient proverbial figure (cf. the Aesopic fable of the spendthrift and the swallow, Perry 169). Timon's aside at TLN 1297-98 ('such summer-birds are men') recycles the simile against the flatterers.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'summer-bird': a bird that appears in summer and is gone in winter; applied figuratively to a fair-weather friend.

The swallow-as-fair-weather-friend is a well-attested classical and proverbial figure, and Timon's aside at TLN 1297-98 explicitly recycles Second Lord's simile as a weapon — the text fully supports the reading.

anchor_text: Alcibiades is banished
summary: Third Lord drops the news that Alcibiades has been banished by Athens. The audience has just seen the Senate do exactly this in Act 3 Scene 5, where Alcibiades pleaded too insistently for a soldier's pardon and was expelled for it. His banishment mirrors Timon's own rejection by the city and sets up his later march on Athens with an army — the public counterpart to Timon's private rage.
detail: Shakespeare derived the Alcibiades plot from Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades (trans. North 1579), though the specific cause — his pleading for a condemned soldier — is an invention; historically, Alcibiades was exiled over the mutilation of the Hermae statues. Plutarch paired the Life of Alcibiades with that of the Roman Coriolanus, another great soldier who turned on his own city, and this structural parallel underlies the play's design. The lords' casual reception of the news ('Alcibiades banished!') — sandwiched between talk of covered dishes and a coming feast — points to the Senate's callousness.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Alcibiades repeatedly exiled and recalled by Athens.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1317

Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades trans. North 1579 is the correct source and publication date, the Alcibiades/Coriolanus pairing in Parallel Lives is confirmed, and the annotation correctly notes that Alcibiades's banishment for pleading a soldier is Shakespeare's invention rather than a claim about Plutarch.

The annotation correctly notes the dramatic function (mirroring Timon's rejection), accurately identifies the historical source-departure (the soldier-pleading cause is Shakespeare's invention, not from Plutarch), and the observation about casual sandwiching between feast-talk is directly borne out by the scene text.

anchor_text: make not a city feast of it, to let the meat cool
summary: A 'city feast' was an official civic banquet of the London guilds and aldermen, notorious for elaborate seating disputes over precedence — who sits where in strict order of rank — that could keep the guests standing and the food cooling for a long time. Timon mockingly tells the lords to sit immediately, as if rank did not matter. The irony is thick: he has already decided to treat them all alike — as nothing.
detail: City feasts were a recognizable Elizabethan institution: the Lord Mayor's Banquet and guild dinners followed strict protocols of precedence (who sat at the high table, who at lower tables) that could become sources of real dispute and delay. Shakespeare invokes the type in a play obsessed with degree and worth: the mock-feast will indeed treat all the guests as equal — equally contemptible. The phrase 'the first place' ('ere we can agree upon / the first place') means the seat of highest honor.

sources.name: Stow, Survey of London
sources.citation: John Stow, A Survey of London (1598), describes the annual feasts of the city companies and their elaborate seating precedence.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1330

Stow's Survey of London (1598) is a real and correctly dated work, but no accessible passage confirming that Stow specifically describes precedence disputes causing food to cool at guild feasts could be verified; the general connection is plausible but the precise supporting claim is unconfirmed.

The city-feast / Lord Mayor's Banquet analogy for seating-precedence delays is a well-documented Elizabethan institution and fits Timon's ironic urging that the lords sit without standing on ceremony; the reading of 'the first place' as the seat of highest honor is philologically standard.

anchor_text: You great benefactors sprinkle our society with thankfulness
summary: Timon delivers what sounds like a table-grace — a prayer of thanks before a meal — but it is a curse in disguise. He addresses the gods as 'great benefactors' but subverts every phrase: 'give, lest your deities be despised' mocks gods who need to keep giving to be respected; 'let a dozen of them be as they are' (of the twelve women) means let half be what they are — prostitutes; 'your foes, O gods! the senators of Athens' finally breaks into open condemnation. The prayer form makes the betrayal all the more savage.
detail: The mock-grace is a precise inversion of the hospitality Timon dispensed in Act 1, where the feast was blessed by Cupid and the gods genuinely praised. Here the form of piety shells out poisonous content: 'borrow of men, men would forsake the gods' parodies the earlier scene where friends would not lend to Timon. The phrase 'as they are' at TLN 1340-41 has a strong sexual implication in context — 'let a dozen of the twelve women be whores as they already are' — though the primary force is the general curse. The rhetorical device of an extended apostrophe to the gods as cover for a series of imprecations is the play's first sample of Timon's sustained curse-rhetoric that will dominate Acts 4-5.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'grace': a short prayer of thanks before a meal.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'benefactor': one who confers benefits; here used with lethal irony.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1333

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon and Onions's Shakespeare Glossary are standard real references, and the lexicographic definitions cited (grace as pre-meal prayer; benefactor as one who confers benefits) accurately reflect those works' scope and content.

The table-grace reading is well-supported — 'The gods require our thanks' (TLN 1332) is the cue, and the annotator correctly notes the subversion-pattern; the claim that 'as they are' carries a sexual implication is appropriately hedged as secondary to the general curse, avoiding overreach.

anchor_text: Uncover, dogs, and lap
summary: 'Uncover' is the command to lift the lids off the serving dishes — the normal signal at a banquet that the food is ready. Instead of food, the uncovered dishes hold only warm water. 'Lap' means to drink by lapping with the tongue, the action of a dog at a bowl. In a single three-word line Timon both reveals the trick and turns the lords from honored guests into dogs licking up scraps.

sources.name: Timon of Athens (First Folio 1623), 3.6
sources.citation: Stage direction in Timon of Athens 3.6 (First Folio 1623): 'The dishes are uncovered' — the dishes prove to hold only warm water (the 'warm water' specification is a standard modern editorial expansion of the Folio's terse direction).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C.T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'lap': to take up liquid with the tongue, as an animal does.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1346

anchor_text: knot of mouth-friends
summary: A 'mouth-friend' is someone who is a friend only with his mouth — in words, in flattery, in protestations at the dinner table — but not in deeds. A 'knot' is a tightly bound cluster or group. The compound is Shakespeare's own coining and one of the play's sharpest phrases: these are men who were friendly only so long as Timon kept feeding them.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mouth-friend': one who professes friendship only by word of mouth; earliest citation is this passage, Timon of Athens 3.6 (so the compound is effectively Shakespeare's coinage).

sources.name: Plutarch, Moralia
sources.citation: Plutarch, 'How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend' (Moralia), Eng. trans. Philemon Holland (1603): the kolax (flatterer) who professes friendship only while the table is loaded, against the true philos.

Rescued in 2026-06-02 review sweep — Corrected the Moralia translator from North to Philemon Holland (1603 English Moralia); OED on the coinage and the flatterer/friend contrast are kept.

The coinage claim ('OED does not record mouth-friend before this passage') and the semantic reading (verbal-only friendship tied to the feast's literal mouth/appetite) are textually sound and directly linked to what Timon has just exposed.

anchor_text: Most smiling, smooth, detested parasites, Courteous destroyers, affable wolves, meek bears
summary: Timon drives his guests out with a rapid-fire catalogue of oxymorons: 'courteous destroyers,' 'affable wolves,' 'meek bears' — each pairs a word of surface politeness with one of predation or danger. 'Trencher-friends' are people who are friendly only at the trencher (a flat wooden plate), i.e., at dinner. 'Time's flies' are like flies that appear in the warmth and vanish with the cold. 'Cap and knee slaves' are flatterers who bow ('cap') and kneel excessively. 'Minute-jacks' are small clock-figures that strike the bell mechanically, used for any servile, clockwork toady.
detail: The oxymoronic structure — 'smiling' + 'detested,' 'courteous' + 'destroyers,' 'affable' + 'wolves' — is Timon's rhetorical signature in this scene and throughout Act 4: the juxtaposition exposes how social surface conceals animal appetite. 'Trencher-friend' (a friend who comes only for the food served on your wooden plate) and 'time's flies' (creatures of the warm season only) are both recorded earliest in this passage; Schmidt and OED cite these lines as primary evidence. 'Minute-jacks' were the little mechanical figures on clock-towers (a famous example was the two Jacquemart figures on the clocktower at Dijon) who struck a bell at each minute; the word became proverbial for a mechanical, servile, tick-by-tick follower of whoever is in power.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'trencher-friend': one who frequents another's table for the sake of the food, earliest citation Timon of Athens 3.6; s.v. 'minute-jack': a figure on a clock that strikes the minutes, figuratively a timeserver.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'cap-and-knee': to pay obsequious reverence; s.v. 'trencher-friends': persons whose friendship is bounded by the table.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1355

OED and Schmidt are real standard references, and the Dijon Jacquemart detail is substantially accurate (the Notre-Dame de Dijon clock does have paired striking figures going back to 1383); no fabrication is present in the supporting sources.

The oxymoron-catalogue reading is fully defensible, but the Dijon Jacquemart claim used to illustrate 'minute-jacks' is a piece of decorative local colour not verifiable from the annotation's own sources and risks being anachronistic or geographically misapplied; the core gloss of 'minute-jacks' as mechanical clock-figures is correct and sufficient without it.

anchor_text: Of man and beast the infinite malady Crust you quite o'er
summary: Timon wishes upon the lords every disease that afflicts both humans and animals — an unlimited, comprehensive infection. 'Crust you quite o'er' means cover you entirely in a crust of scabs or scale, as plague, pox, and mange do to skin. The phrasing anticipates the venereal-disease curses Timon heaps on Alcibiades's mistresses in Act 4, and shows that the misanthropic curse has already reached the totality it will sustain for the rest of the play.
detail: In the early modern medical understanding, many skin diseases (plague buboes, syphilitic sores, leprous crusts) were visible eruptions of inner corruption. 'Crust o'er' recalls the physical symptoms of the 'French disease' (syphilis), which by the early 17th century had acquired a whole vocabulary of scaling and crusting. The word 'infinite' is typical of Timon's escalating rhetoric: nothing partial or selective — not just a sickness but ALL sickness, ALL diseases of ALL creatures, ALL at once. Lucian's Timon (the Misanthrope) is already using currency-disease metaphors; Shakespeare drives the imagery toward the body itself.

sources.name: Lucian, Timon (Misanthrope)
sources.citation: Lucian of Samosata, Timon, or the Misanthrope (2nd c. AD): Timon's extended curses on the flattering crowd who return to seek his new-found gold.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'crust': to cover with a hard coating; used of scabrous or syphilitic sores forming an outer shell on the body.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1359

Lucian's Timon (Misanthrope) is a real source and does feature Timon confronting a returning crowd, but the characterisation of Lucian's text as using 'currency-disease metaphors' is not supported by the dialogue, which depicts physical violence (beating with a spade) rather than disease imagery; the OED claim for 'crust' is plausible but unverifiable without direct OED access.

The reading of 'crust you quite o'er' as scaling/scabbing disease-imagery (pox, mange, leprosy) is standard and the text fully supports a general-disease rather than specifically venereal reading; the venereal sub-reading is appropriately presented as anticipatory rather than primary.

anchor_text: Henceforth be no feast, Whereat a villain's not a welcome guest
summary: Timon ends with a rhymed couplet that twists a truism: a proper feast excludes villains, but Timon says there should be NO feast at which a villain is NOT welcome — meaning every feast is now made for villains, because all men are villains. The syntax requires a double negative. His next couplet, 'Burn, house! sink Athens! henceforth hated be / Of Timon man and all humanity!', is a formal curse-declaration that closes his life as an Athenian citizen.
detail: The shift to rhyming couplets signals Timon's exit from social prose into the harder, more formal register of the curse. The construction 'be no X, whereat a Y is not welcome' is a logical inversion: Timon is not excluding villains from future feasts; he is saying all future feasts should invite them. The statement encodes his new creed — society is now wholly villainous — and the two closing couplets are the play's formal pivot. After line 1366 Timon leaves Athens and never returns alive; the last couplet ('hated be / Of Timon man and all humanity') sounds like the end of a de casibus poem — the great man fallen and cursing the world. The anonymous academic Timon play (c. 1601-02) has a comparable exit-curse.

sources.name: Boccaccio, De Casibus (and Mirror for Magistrates)
sources.citation: Boccaccio, De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360); John Lydgate, Fall of Princes (1431-38); A Mirror for Magistrates (1559): the de casibus tradition of formal curse-speeches at the point of a great man's fall.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1363

Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium, Lydgate's Fall of Princes, and A Mirror for Magistrates are all real and correctly described works within the de casibus tradition, and 'c. 1360' falls within the confirmed composition range (1355-1374) for the Boccaccio.

The double-negative syntax reading is correct and the pivot-to-couplets observation is sound, but invoking the de casibus tradition as the frame for these two exit couplets is an interpretive reach — the lines function as a curse-declaration and formal exit but lack the retrospective great-man-fall narration that defines de casibus; the reference card link to de-casibus-tragedy and fortunes-wheel adds apparatus not clearly earned by two closing couplets.

anchor_text: Matrons, turn incontinent
summary: 'Incontinent' here means sexually unchaste — unable to restrain one's desires. Timon curses Athens's respectable married women (matrons) to become promiscuous. The word has nothing to do with its modern medical meaning.

anchor_text: Degrees, observances, customs and laws, Decline to your confounding contraries
summary: Timon recites a catalogue of the pillars of organized society — social ranks ('degrees'), religious duties ('piety'), family bonds, civic order, trades — and then curses every one to collapse into its opposite ('confounding contraries'). The structure is an anti-benediction: a prayer that the entire social order unmake itself.
detail: 'Degrees' is the technical term for the hierarchical ranks of society: king above noble, noble above gentleman, and so on down through commons to servants — the Elizabethan doctrine of order often called 'the great chain of being.' The word recurs famously in Ulysses's speech on 'degree' in Troilus and Cressida: 'Take but degree away, untune that string, / And hark what discord follows.' Timon's speech is that discord spoken as a deliberate curse. 'Confounding contraries' means the opposites that undo and destroy (Latin confundere, to mix up, ruin). The rhetorical device is climax followed by catastrophe: Shakespeare builds the long anaphoric list (Piety ... Religion ... peace ... justice ... truth ... Domestic awe ... Instruction, manners, mysteries and trades / Degrees, observances, customs and laws) only to curse the whole edifice to ruin in a single verb. The speech has been read as the most radical statement of social nihilism in the Shakespearean canon.

sources.name: Homily Against Disobedience (1571)
sources.citation: Certain Sermons or Homilies Appointed to be Read in Churches: 'An Homily Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion' (1571) — the official statement of social order through 'degree' that Timon's catalogue inverts.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'degree' (rank in the social hierarchy) and 'confound' (to ruin, destroy, bring to nothing).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1399

The Homily Against Disobedience is a real document and an accurate parallel for 'degree' ideology (it was composed 1570 and printed 1571, so the 1571 date in the citation is defensible for the printed text); the Schmidt citation is genuine; the Troilus and Cressida 'degree' parallel is accurate and standard scholarship.

The identification of 'degrees' with the doctrine of hierarchical social order is sound, the Troilus and Cressida parallel is apt, and the characterization of the speech as anti-benediction or social-nihilism catalogue is a mainstream, defensible reading; the rhetorical description is accurate.

anchor_text: Itches, blains, Sow all the Athenian bosoms, and their crop Be general leprosy
summary: 'Blains' are pustules or blisters on the skin — inflamed, weeping sores. Timon prays that disease be literally sown across Athens like seed-grain, its harvest being 'general leprosy' (epidemic skin disease). The agricultural metaphor — sow, crop — gives the curse a grotesque fertility inversion: instead of bread, a plague harvest.
detail: A 'blain' (also 'blane') is a pustule, blister, or skin sore. The image echoes the sixth plague of Egypt, which the Geneva Bible (1599) renders as 'a scab breaking out into blisters upon man, and upon beast' (Exodus 9:9-10) — the same boils-and-sores affliction Timon wishes on the city. 'Leprosy' in early modern usage covered a range of visible skin diseases, not necessarily Hansen's disease; the key was that it marked the sufferer visibly as unclean and outcast. The agricultural conceit (sow/crop) in a disease curse is bitter irony: Timon, the once-lavish host and giver, now prays for a harvest of rot. The same disease-curse structure continues into 4.3, where Timon heaps venereal disease on Alcibiades's mistresses in language far more explicit.

anchor_text: Such a house broke! So noble a master fall'n
summary: 'House broke' means the household has gone bankrupt and disbanded — the entire establishment, with its servants, debts, and social obligations, has collapsed at once. In early modern usage a 'house' was both the building and the institution it contained; when it 'broke,' it dissolved like a failed business. The First Servant's exclamation registers both financial ruin and the dismantling of a whole social world.
detail: The commercial sense of 'break' (to become insolvent) was current in Shakespeare's London, where merchants' houses 'broke' when they could not meet their debts — a disgrace that attached to every person associated with them. The servants' scene makes the ruin collective: they too are 'undone' because their identity and livelihood were bound to Timon's household. The OED records 'break' in the financial sense from the mid-sixteenth century (OED s.v. 'break' v., sense 55a).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1427

The commercial sense of 'break' (go bankrupt) is well-attested and the context — servants lamenting 'undone,' 'nothing remaining' — confirms a financial-ruin reading; the extension to the whole household institution is sound.

anchor_text: As we do turn our backs From our companion, thrown into his grave
summary: The Second Servant builds an extended simile comparing Timon's false friends to mourners at a burial: just as people turn away from a coffin once it is in the ground and walk off, leaving their promises of remembrance behind with the corpse, so Timon's 'familiars' (close friends) have abandoned him the moment his fortune was 'buried.' The simile equates financial ruin with death, and Timon's friends with hollow graveside mourners.
detail: 'Familiars' here means intimate friends or household companions, carrying the same meaning as the Latin familiares — those of the same familia (household). The compressed phrase 'Like empty purses pick'd' extends the metaphor: the false friends, once they have extracted everything from Timon, are as empty as a pickpocket's discarded wallet. 'Dedicated beggar to the air' (TLN 1436) — consigned wholly to the open air, utterly homeless — clinches the simile by completing the picture of someone left with nothing but sky above him. The rhetorical device is a formal simile (introduced by 'As'), sustained over seven lines, which was the kind of extended comparison Shakespeare drew from Virgil's Aeneid and from Ovid.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1431

The sustained grave-to-burial simile is clearly present in the text, 'familiars' as intimate companions is standard, and 'empty purses pick'd' as an extension of the friends-as-pickpockets image is supported by the surrounding lines; the passing Virgil/Ovid attribution for the extended-simile form is vague but does not distort the core reading.

anchor_text: Leak'd is our bark, And we, poor mates, stand on the dying deck
summary: The Third Servant compares Timon's ruined household to a sinking ship: the vessel ('bark') has sprung a leak, the 'mates' (sailors, but also fellow servants) stand on the sinking deck listening to the waves, and they must all 'part / Into this sea of air' — scatter into the open world like a crew abandoning ship. The sea-wreck image turns a financial collapse into a vivid physical disaster.
detail: A 'bark' (or 'barque') was a small sailing vessel; 'mates' were the officers or crew. 'The dying deck' compresses two meanings: a deck where men are dying, and a deck in the act of dying (sinking). 'Part into this sea of air' is the most striking phrase — the servants will disperse into the open air the way wreckage scatters across the sea, each piece going its own way. Elizabethan audiences were familiar with shipwreck as a figure for sudden ruin; Shakespeare uses it across the canon (Othello, The Tempest, The Comedy of Errors), but here it is the servants, not the master, who stand at the broken rail.

The leaking-ship image is explicit in the text; 'bark,' 'mates,' 'surges,' and 'dying deck' are accurately glossed, and 'part into this sea of air' as dispersal into the open world is the natural reading of the phrase.

anchor_text: mock'd with glory? or so live, But in a dream of friendship? To have his pomp, and all what state compounds But only painted
summary: Flavius uses 'painted' to mean both literally painted (like a portrait or a stage-flat) and falsely varnished over — the same word the text applies to Timon's false friends ('his varnish'd friends' follows immediately). A 'painted' friend is one who looks real but is a surface image with nothing behind it. 'All what state compounds' means everything that high social rank is made of — the pomp, the attendants, the feasts — all of it was only a painted illusion, not substance. The phrase 'dream of friendship' reinforces the idea: Timon's entire social world was a fiction he mistook for reality.
detail: The association of paint with deception is pervasive in Shakespeare — Hamlet cries 'God hath given you one face, and you make yourselves another' (3.1), and Timon himself will later heap contempt on the Painter who returns hoping for gold (5.1). 'Varnish'd friends' (TLN 1460) layers a second coating metaphor: varnish is a protective gloss applied to wood, bright-looking but still only a surface. Together 'painted' and 'varnish'd' frame Flavius's meditation on how completely Timon confused appearance with reality, a theme the play has been pursuing since the flatterers' opening scenes.

anchor_text: Undone by goodness. Strange, unusual blood, When man's worst sin is he does too much good! Who then dares to be half so kind agen? For bounty, that makes gods, does still mar men.
summary: Flavius identifies the paradox at the heart of the play: Timon's ruin was caused not by vice but by excess generosity — 'bounty' so great that it is described as godlike, yet it destroyed him as a man. In classical and biblical tradition, the gods were defined by their giving without limit; Timon tried to live that way among humans and was bankrupted. 'Strange, unusual blood' means an extraordinary nature or temperament — 'blood' in this usage means one's innate character or disposition.
detail: The phrase 'bounty, that makes gods' draws on the ancient commonplace that boundless giving is a divine attribute. The play inherits its conception of Timon's mythically excessive generosity from Lucian's dialogue 'Timon, or the Misanthrope,' where the gods note how lavishly Timon once gave — though Lucian frames that giving as folly rather than virtue, the very paradox Flavius is struggling with here. 'Mar' means to spoil or ruin (Old English mierran); the contrast with 'make' ('makes gods' versus 'mar men') is a deliberate chiasm. Flavius's bewilderment is that the flaw which undoes Timon is not a vice but virtue carried past human limit.

anchor_text: O blessed breeding sun! draw from the earth
summary: Timon begins his first great wilderness soliloquy by invoking the sun not as a life-giver but as a weapon — he commands it to suck up disease from the earth and infect the air. The apostrophe (direct address to an absent thing) launches a sustained curse against all created life.
detail: The opening reverses the sun's traditional role as the source of growth and warmth; Timon wants it to function as a giant still that distills the earth's 'rotten humidity' into airborne plague. This is consistent with the play's inversion of all positive values: generosity becomes misanthropy, feast becomes starvation, gold becomes poison. The sun-as-instrument-of-destruction also frames Timon as a kind of anti-god, commandeering natural forces for destruction rather than creation.

anchor_text: below thy sister's orb
summary: The sun's 'sister' is the moon; in classical cosmology the sun and moon were sibling deities — Helios (the sun) and Selene (the moon), both children of the Titan Hyperion. Timon is telling the sun to poison the sub-lunar air, the region between the moon and the earth.
detail: In ancient and medieval cosmology the sphere just below the moon was the boundary between the incorruptible heavens and the corruptible sublunary world of matter and disease; to poison the 'air' in this region is to corrupt the whole zone of mortal life. Hesiod names Helios and Selene among the children of Hyperion and Theia (Theogony 371-374).

anchor_text: every grize of fortune / Is smooth'd by that below
summary: 'Grize' (also spelled 'grise' or 'greese') means a step of a staircase. Timon says that every step on fortune's ladder is kept smooth by the fawning of whoever stands one step lower — flattery flows upward through every level of society.
detail: The stair-image connects to Fortune's wheel and the social hierarchy: each rank flatters the one above it to advance. 'The learned pate / Ducks to the golden fool' (TLN 1492-93) follows directly — even scholars bow to wealthy idiots. This extends the metaphor: knowledge itself is prostituted to money. The image is closely linked to Ulysses's 'degree' speech in Troilus and Cressida, another satiric vision of hierarchy.

anchor_text: His semblable, yea, himself, Timon disdains
summary: 'Semblable' (from French semblable, 'like') means one's likeness, double, or fellow — any person who resembles oneself. It is the logical endpoint of misanthropy: Timon is himself a man, so complete hatred of mankind must include self-hatred.

anchor_text: Destruction fang mankind

anchor_text: I am no idle votarist
summary: A 'votarist' is a person who has made a vow — a devotee, a monk or nun. Timon is saying he is not a false worshipper when he calls on the heavens for roots: he genuinely needs them and will not be fobbed off with gold. The irony is that he has just found a hoard of the gold he despises.

anchor_text: This yellow slave / Will knit and break religions
summary: Timon calls gold a 'yellow slave' — its color identifies it, but 'slave' inverts the usual power relation, making gold (which enslaves people) itself a slave to anyone who possesses it. summary: 'Hoar' means white or grey-white with age, frost, or disease. A 'spital-house' is a hospital or hospice, especially one for the diseased and destitute. 'Cast the gorge' means to vomit. summary: 'Embalms' here means to perfume or preserve, making fragrant what would otherwise decay — the same word used for preserving a corpse. anchor_text: I am Misanthropos, and hate mankind
summary: 'Misanthropos' is the Greek word for man-hater: 'misanthr-' (from Greek 'misein,' to hate, and 'anthropos,' mankind). Timon uses it as a name for himself, directly invoking the classical tradition of Timon as the archetypal hater of humanity. Lucian's dialogue 'Timon, or the Misanthrope' made this name famous in antiquity and is one of the play's key sources.
detail: By naming himself 'Misanthropos' Timon acknowledges that he has become the legendary type, the proverbial man-hater of antiquity. Lucian's Timon (2nd century AD) is a ruined rich man who turns to digging and curses the friends who abandoned him; Plutarch's Life of Antony (ch. 70) reports the same tradition. The self-naming is simultaneously a moment of tragic self-knowledge and a dark irony: Timon names himself after the literary tradition he is now enacting.

anchor_text: This fell whore of thine / Hath in her more destruction than thy sword / For all her cherubin look
summary: Timon addresses Phrynia as a 'fell' (fierce, savage) whore, saying she carries more destructive power in her body than Alcibiades's sword, despite her angel-like ('cherubin') appearance. This reflects a standard early modern claim that venereal disease — the primary vehicle of this destruction in the play's imagination — killed more men than war did. The note must be read as clinical description of the text's misogyny, not endorsement.
detail: The 'destruction' Timon refers to is primarily venereal disease, which the early modern period associated both with sex workers and with military campaigns (soldiers infected in brothels). The 'cherubin look' echoes the conventional trope of the beautiful temptress concealing moral danger — the devil in angelic form. Timon's cursing of Phrynia and Timandra throughout this scene is violently misogynistic in its content; the annotations record the text's rhetoric as historical evidence, not as endorsement. anchor_text: Thy lips rot off! / I will not kiss thee; then the rot returns / To thine own lips again
summary: Phrynia curses Timon that his lips will rot off; he replies that he will not kiss her because the 'rot' (syphilis or other venereal disease) would then rebound to her. 'The rot' was common Elizabethan slang for venereal disease, particularly syphilis, whose advanced stages could destroy soft tissue including the nose and lips. Timon implies that the disease already belongs to her and he would merely be returning it.
detail: The exchange is the play's most explicit invocation of venereal disease as a weapon in the gender war Timon wages on these women. The dramatic logic is: Phrynia is imagined as a carrier of disease who passes it to her clients; kissing her would infect Timon; he refuses, so the curse bounces back. The pun on 'rot' for both moral and physical decay is typical of this scene's strategy of fusing ethical and medical disgust. These curses are the text's material; the historical context is early modern moral and medical discourse on prostitution, not a position endorsed by the annotations.

anchor_text: As the moon does, by wanting light to give: / But then renew I could not like the moon; / There were no suns to borrow of
summary: Timon explains his transformation through a compressed astronomical simile: the moon wanes when it has no light to give, but renews itself by borrowing from the sun. Timon waned the same way — by giving out everything. But unlike the moon, he could not renew, because there were no 'suns' (generous friends) to borrow light from. The simile reduces the play's plot to three lines.
detail: The moon's borrowed light was a commonplace of Renaissance cosmology (Aristotle, the Ptolemaic system) and a standard emblem of dependence and reflection. Timon, who was himself the sun-like figure of generosity at the center of Athens's social system, finds his light was also borrowed — from the false friends who left him in the dark. anchor_text: Willing misery / Outlives incertain pomp, is crown'd before; / The one is filling still, never complete; / The other, at high wish

anchor_text: Promising is the very air o' the time
summary: The Painter delivers a miniature satiric essay: promising has replaced performing as the currency of social life. Performance (actually doing what you said) is 'ever the duller for his act' — it is flat and anticlimactic next to the bright hope of a promise. Only simple, unglamorous people still bother to keep their word; in polite society a promise is treated like a will or testament, a sign you are so near death you had better settle your affairs.
detail: The speech is a set-piece of Jacobean social satire on courtly insincerity. 'The deed of saying is quite out of use' puns on 'deed' (an act, and a legal document): the very word for action has become an antique. 'Will or testament' sharpens the joke: a will is what you write when you have given up on life; only a man of poor judgment — or near the grave — actually fulfills his promises. The Painter himself is demonstrating the thesis: he has come to Timon promising 'an excellent piece' he has no intention of delivering unless he is paid first. Timon, listening aside, has already grasped the irony.

anchor_text: Thou canst not paint a man so bad as is thyself
summary: Timon plays on the Painter's trade: no matter how wicked a subject the Painter depicts in his art, the man doing the painting is worse. 'Paint' also carried the secondary sense of 'disguise with cosmetics' — to cover over one's true, ugly nature. Both meanings apply: the Painter cannot represent villainy because he embodies it.
detail: The pun on 'paint' (artistic representation vs. cosmetic concealment) was a standard satiric device. Anti-cosmetic literature of the period argued that painted faces were a form of moral fraud; here Timon extends the charge to the painter's professional skill itself — the craftsman of surfaces is himself all surface. The aside is spoken before Timon reveals himself, so it functions as dramatic irony: we hear Timon's real verdict on men who present themselves as honest friends.

anchor_text: a satire against the softness of prosperity, with a discovery of the infinite flatteries
summary: The Poet plans to write a verse satire depicting Timon himself as its hero — a person who, at the height of luxury, was undone by flatterers. This mirrors the Poet's own earlier poem in Act 1 (a fable of Fortune's hill and the turning away of the crowd). The cynical scheme: pitch to a patron a poem about his own fall, then collect the patronage fee.
detail: Verse satire was a live and contentious genre in the 1590s and early 1600s (Hall, Marston, Donne); the bishops had it publicly burned in 1599. A 'personating' poem — one that depicted a recognizable individual — occupied legally and ethically dangerous territory; it could be construed as libel. The Poet's plan to write a satire about Timon's victimization by flatterers, while himself attempting to be one of those flatterers, is the scene's central irony. Timon's aside ('Wilt thou whip thine own faults in other men?') identifies it precisely: the satirist attacks in verse the vice he is himself practicing.

anchor_text: What a god's gold, That he is worshipp'd in a baser temple Than where swine feed
summary: Timon frames gold as a pagan god who accepts worship in any sty, no matter how filthy. Calling the greedy Poet and Painter a 'temple' for gold-worship, and a baser one than a pigsty, compresses his disgust: at least pigs are honestly beastly. The speech is a sardonic parody of religious devotion.
detail: The image develops a long tradition of equating avarice with idolatry. Timon turns the irony against himself as much as against the parasites: he once was the high priest of gold's temple in Athens, the magnificent host. Now, watching others scramble for what he has dug out of the earth, he sees the worship of money as pure paganism, the god of gold demanding obeisance in the most degraded 'temples' — human greed — rather than proper shrines. 'Baser than where swine feed' also echoes the parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:15–16), where the son's lowest degradation is feeding pigs; the allusion may be half-conscious in the playwright's language.

anchor_text: 'Tis thou that rigg'st the bark and plough'st the foam, Settlest admired reverence in a slave
summary: Timon apostrophizes gold as the power that equips ships ('rigg'st the bark'), drives sea trade, and makes even a slave command respect. 'Plough'st the foam' is a metaphor for sailing: a ship's prow cuts through the sea as a plough cuts earth. Gold, Timon says, is the real force behind every human enterprise and every false distinction of rank.
detail: The apostrophe to gold — a direct address to an abstract force as if it were a person present — is a formal rhetorical device (prosopopoeia). The image of gold as the power that launches ships recalls the classical association of trade and greed; 'rigging' a bark requires timber, cordage, sailcloth, all purchased with money. 'Settlest admired reverence in a slave' is the bitterest cut: gold can make the lowest social rank appear noble. The speech closely parallels Timon's famous gold-apostrophe at 4.3.26–40 ('O thou sweet king-killer'), which the play uses twice — once in furious hatred, once in this more compressed, aside form.

anchor_text: thy saints for aye Be crown'd with plagues
summary: Timon inverts the language of religious worship: gold's 'saints' — those who venerate it alone — deserve not heavenly crowns but plague-crowns forever. 'For aye' means for ever. The blessing-as-curse form is a feature of Timon's sustained misanthropic rhetoric throughout Acts 4 and 5 — he offers what looks like a benediction and reverses it into malediction. The image anticipates his later commands to Alcibiades's mistresses to spread venereal disease through the city as a form of divine punishment.

anchor_text: Have I once liv'd to see two honest men
summary: The line is savage irony. Timon already knows from overhearing the Poet and Painter that they are the opposite of honest. Calling them 'honest' to their faces is a trap: he will repeat the word so insistently ('honest men,' 'honest men,' 'ye're honest men') that it becomes an accusation. The audience shares his private joke.

By the time he says 'Ye're honest men! Ye've heard that I have gold; / I am sure you have. Speak truth; ye're honest men' the repeated word has been drained of content and refilled with contempt. The structural irony is sustained for nearly thirty lines — among the longest ironic builds in the play.

anchor_text: for thy fiction, Why, thy verse swells with stuff so fine and smooth That thou art even natural in thine art
summary: 'Fiction' here means literary invention or the Poet's devised poem, but it also means a lie. 'Natural' is another trap: to the Poet it sounds like high praise (naturally talented, born to the art); it also means foolish — a 'natural' was an Elizabethan term for an idiot or simpleton. Timon is calling the Poet an instinctive liar and a born fool at the same time.

'So fine and smooth' parodies the compliments flatterers pay to verse: 'fine' and 'smooth' are the vocabulary of praise for polished, courtly writing. 'Natural in thine art' then inverts the Poet's probable self-image as a sophisticated artist: Timon implies he doesn't even have to try — knavery and flattery come to him as naturally as breath.

anchor_text: you hear him cog, see him dissemble, Know his gross patchery
summary: 'Cog' means to cheat or deceive, especially by wheedling flattery; 'dissemble' means to hide true intentions behind a false front; 'patchery' means shabby trickery, fraud — literally the work of a 'patch,' a fool or a botcher. Timon is saying: you know the knave in your company is a liar, a fake, and a cheap cheat — yet you feed him and keep him close.

'Gross patchery' — clumsy, obvious fraud — is the sharpest insult: the knave is not even a skilled deceiver. The passage is directed ostensibly at a hypothetical 'knave' in the Poet's and Painter's circle, but structurally it describes the Poet and Painter themselves, whom Timon has just called 'honest men' nineteen times to their faces.

anchor_text: Yet an arch-villain keeps him company
summary: The logical trap snaps shut: Timon told both men to go separate ways and rid themselves of their knave. Each man apart is alone — and yet, Timon says, an arch-villain keeps each one company. Therefore the villain must be the man himself. This is a classic enthymeme, a compressed syllogism: the premise (a villain accompanies you wherever you go) forces the conclusion without Timon having to state it.
detail: The rhetorical structure is Socratic: question, concession, reductio. Timon then completes the trap in the following two lines: if you, Painter, go where you are, and two villains shall not be there — don't come near yourself. The joke holds for a beat before the expulsion, making the Poet and Painter complicit in their own exposure: they confirmed the accusation by denying it so eagerly. The device mirrors Timon's earlier sustained irony about their 'honesty.'

anchor_text: You are an alchemist; make gold of that
summary: An alchemist claimed the ability to transmute base metals into gold — a widespread pursuit in the medieval and early modern period. Timon throws the Poet a handful of coins (or perhaps just beats him), telling him sarcastically that if he is such a skilled transformer of reality he can make gold out of this worthless encounter. The insult identifies the Poet's flattering verse with the alchemist's empty promises of transformation.
detail: Alchemy was still taken seriously in some quarters in the early 1600s (Ben Jonson's The Alchemist, 1610, is its definitive satiric treatment), but it was also the byword for charlatanism and false promises of wealth. The parallel is exact: the Poet promised Timon 'an intent that's coming toward him' — a poem not yet written, a future gift; the alchemist promised gold not yet made. Both are professionals of anticipated value that never materialises. Timon, who now despises the gold he has actually dug from the earth, finds the analogy savagely comic.

anchor_text: Thou sun that comfort'st, burn!
summary: Timon's first words to the senators invert a natural blessing: the sun, which warms and sustains life, is commanded to burn instead of comfort. The pattern is typical of his late misanthropic speech — turning the expected gift (warmth, light, hospitality, gold) into its destructive opposite. Every good thing, in Timon's vision, should become a weapon.

Here it is compressed into four words at the opening of his only exchange with the senators. Dramatically it signals immediately that no persuasion is possible: a man who wishes the sun would burn instead of shine is not going to be talked back to civic duty. The image may glance at the classical Phaethon myth — the reckless driver who caused the sun to scorch the earth — though the allusion is implicit rather than named.

anchor_text: each true word, a blister! and each false Be as a cauterizing to the root o' the tongue
summary: Timon curses both true speech and false speech equally: tell the truth and get a blister; tell a lie and have your tongue cauterized (burned closed at the root with a hot iron). Either way, language itself should be physically punished and shut down. The curse turns Timon's own final farewell speech — which ends 'language end' — into a form of self-fulfilling prophecy.

The curse is symmetrically total: not one outcome (lies punished) but both outcomes (truth punished too). This totalizing, both-directions rage is Timon's rhetorical signature — there is no escape through virtue, because virtue is as suspect as vice. The logic anticipates his final epitaph: 'Seek not my name: a plague consume you wicked caitiffs left.'

anchor_text: would send them back the plague, Could I but catch it for them
summary: Bubonic plague was a live and recurring terror in Elizabethan and Jacobean London, closing theatres and killing thousands (severe outbreaks in 1592–93, 1603, 1609). To wish plague on someone was the harshest available malediction. Timon's regret that he cannot infect himself to give it to the senators crystallises the depth of his misanthropy: he would willingly die of plague to transmit it to his enemies.
detail: Plague curses run through the whole second half of the play and are Timon's characteristic register. The joke here (I'd catch it for you) has a black comedy the senators clearly cannot appreciate: the offer to bring a gift — 'would send them back' — mimics the language of return gifts and hospitality, but the gift is pestilence. The Timon of Athens was possibly written in or near 1607–08, another bad plague year; the repeated invocations of plague as the fitting end for a corrupt city may carry particular topical weight for an audience that knew the disease personally.

anchor_text: There's not a whittle in the unruly camp But I do prize it at my love before The reverend'st throat in Athens
summary: A 'whittle' is a small knife or clasp-knife — the most ordinary, cheap cutting implement a soldier might carry. The contrast of the smallest weapon against the most revered life measures his total contempt for the city's dignitaries.

Setting it above 'the reverend'st throat in Athens' (the most venerable senator, whose throat would be cut) makes the contempt geometrically precise. anchor_text: I was writing of my epitaph; It will be seen to-morrow. My long sickness Of health and living now begins to mend, And nothing brings me all things
summary: Timon announces that he is composing his own epitaph — the inscription for his tomb — and will be dead by tomorrow. The 'long sickness of health and living' is a paradox: he has been ill for as long as he was alive and well; his life itself was the disease, and death is the cure. 'Nothing brings me all things' means that having nothing (death, nothingness) is the condition that gives him everything he wants — which is for the world to leave him alone.
detail: Timon's epitaph is reported by a soldier in 5.4 and read by Alcibiades; it appears in two versions in Plutarch's Life of Antony (North 1579, ch. 70), both cursing all who pass. The detail of a man writing his own epitaph was already associated with Timon in antiquity (Plutarch mentions two competing epitaphs attributed to him and to Callimachus). 'Long sickness of health and living' is one of the play's most compressed paradoxes: the entire arc of the drama — Timon's philanthropic prosperity as the real catastrophe, misanthropy as the cure — is compressed into nine words.

anchor_text: I have a tree, which grows here in my close, That mine own use invites me to cut down, And shortly must I fell it. Tell my friends, Tell Athens, in the sequence of degree From high to low throughout, that whoso please To stop affliction, let him take his haste, Come hither, ere my tree hath felt the axe, And hang himself
summary: The 'tree for hanging' is the play's darkest satiric joke. Timon offers a public service: whoever wants to escape life's miseries can come to his grove and use his tree as a gallows before he cuts it down. Lucian's dialogue 'Timon, or the Misanthrope' contains a similar mock-invitation, and the tree-for-hanging appears in Plutarch's Life of Antony as a detail of the historical Timon's legend.
detail: In Plutarch (North 1579, ch. 70), Timon publicly announces that he has a tree he is about to cut down and invites anyone who wants to hang himself to do so while the tree still stands — a joke that was already ancient and attributed to Timon in the classical sources. Lucian's satirical dialogue (Timon, or the Misanthrope) dramatises Timon's bitter humor at length. Shakespeare gives the speech a careful social architecture: 'in the sequence of degree / From high to low throughout' means from the highest senators to the lowest citizens — all are equally invited to hang themselves. The universalism is the point: this is not political satire of the great; it is misanthropy that encompasses the whole species.

anchor_text: Timon hath made his everlasting mansion Upon the beached verge of the salt flood, Who once a day with his embossed froth The turbulent surge shall cover

'Everlasting mansion' (eternal dwelling-place, i.e. a tomb) placed at the tide-line is drawn from Plutarch, who specifies that Timon was buried by the sea at Halae. 'Embossed froth' means foaming, swelling surf. The sea grave refuses the city entirely — not even land will hold him.

The detail of the daily tidal covering is Shakespeare's poetic elaboration, transforming a biographical note into an image of perfect, perpetual isolation. 'Beached verge' (the edge, the margin) also carries the sense of a liminal space - neither land nor sea, neither life nor death.

anchor_text: Lips, let sour words go by and language end: What is amiss, plague and infection mend! Graves only be men's works and death their gain! Sun, hide thy beams! Timon hath done his reign
summary: Timon's last spoken words are a formal valediction structured as four rhyming couplets that successively close down speech, cure, human achievement, and daylight. 'Language end' calls for the end of language itself — all of it, not just dishonest speech. 'Plague and infection mend' inverts the wish for healing: only disease can fix what is wrong with the world. 'Timon hath done his reign' treats his life as a kingly rule now finished, and exits into the cave.
detail: The rhetorical structure is a formal cursing-valediction, each couplet extinguishing something previously valued: words (language), medicine (mend), human works, sunlight. The repetition of the imperative ('let,' 'mend,' 'be,' 'hide') makes the speech sound like a decree. 'Reign' is a charged word for a man who explicitly refused the senators' offer of effective political power moments earlier: he gives himself the kingship at the moment of death, but his kingdom is nothingness. The final exit into the cave — from which he does not return alive — completes the trajectory from banqueting lord of Athens to a man whose only dwelling is a dark hole in a rock.

anchor_text: His fellowship i' the cause against your city
summary: Alcibiades is sending letters to Timon asking him to join the military campaign against Athens. This mirrors the historical Alcibiades of Plutarch, who was banished by Athens and marched on the city that had wronged him — just as Timon, though in self-imposed exile, was also abandoned by Athens's citizens. The Messenger has intercepted a courier carrying these letters to Timon's cave.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades (trans. North, 1579) supplied Shakespeare and Middleton with the figure of the great soldier turned against his own ungrateful city. In Plutarch, Alcibiades repeatedly defected and returned; here his appeal to Timon is dramatically important because it shows the two men's fates are still intertwined — Timon's bitter gold has already funded Alcibiades's war (4.3), and the letters suggest Alcibiades wants Timon's active participation, not just his money. The phrase 'in part for his sake' (TLN 2301) confirms that Alcibiades is making Timon's personal grievance one of the war's stated causes, not merely a pretext.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades (North 1579)

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2300

Linking Alcibiades's letter to Plutarch's banished general is legitimate, and the claim that Timon's gold funded the campaign in 4.3 is textually accurate, but the annotation overstates 'fellowship' as a call for Timon's 'active participation' — the letters solicit his nominal alliance and use of his grievance as political justification, not personal military service from a cave-dwelling misanthrope.

anchor_text: hath outstretch'd his span
summary: 'Span' is the measured length of a human life — from the Old English 'spann,' a hand's breadth used as a unit of measurement. To say Timon has 'outstretch'd his span' means he has lived out his allotted time and is now dead. The soldier is reading the epitaph and relaying its claim.
detail: The word 'span' carries a biblical resonance (Psalm 39:5, Geneva 1599: 'thou hast made my days as a span long') where God fixes the brevity of human life. Here the formula is the epitaph's own claim — Timon has completed, even exceeded, his appointed time — which sits with bitter irony against the violence of his self-chosen exile and death. The Soldier treats the statement as a simple factual report from the inscription.

anchor_text: the character I'll take with wax
summary: 'Character' here means written letters or an inscription, not a person in a story. The Soldier cannot read the script on Timon's tomb, so he presses wax against the stone to take a physical impression of the letters and carry it to Alcibiades, who can decipher it.
detail: The word 'character' (from Greek 'kharaktēr,' an engraved mark) meant any form of writing, lettering, or cipher in Elizabethan English. Taking a wax impression of an inscription was a practical method for copying text from stone monuments that the copyist could not themselves read — used by travelers, antiquarians, and soldiers in the field. The device is dramaturgically useful: it delays the audience's hearing of Timon's epitaph until 5.4, when Alcibiades reads it aloud before Athens's gates, giving the words maximum weight at the play's climax.

'Character' as inscription/lettering is standard Elizabethan usage, the wax-impression technique is historically plausible, and the dramaturgical explanation about deferring the epitaph reading to 5.4 is accurate and not an overreach.

anchor_text: hath in every figure skill, / An ag'd interpreter, though young in days
summary: 'Figure' means any written character, letter, or numeral — not a person. The Soldier praises Alcibiades as someone skilled in reading every kind of writing, and calls him 'an aged interpreter though young in days': he reads with the wisdom of an experienced scholar despite his youth.
detail: The phrase neatly encapsulates Alcibiades's reputation in Plutarch as an educated, many-talented general. 'Figure' (from Latin 'figura') covered numerical figures, written letters, and rhetorical forms — here it means any symbol carved on the tomb. 'Ag'd interpreter' is an oxymoron that flatters Alcibiades: the wisdom of age in a young man's body. The compliment also functions as exposition, preparing the audience for the literate general who will read the wax impression aloud in the next scene.

anchor_text: Now the time is flush, When crouching marrow
summary: 'Flush' here means fully ripe, ready, or at the full — the moment of peak readiness. Alcibiades says the time has now come to capacity: even the marrow (the innermost strength of the bones, i.e., the deepest, most patient endurance) can hold no more and cries 'No more!'

The double image — brimming liquid and bone-deep patience at its limit — captures the moment Alcibiades's long-suppressed anger tips into action.

anchor_text: pursy insolence shall break his wind
summary: 'Pursy' means fat, short of breath, and puffed up — a swollen, wheezy person who has over-indulged. The image reduces their proud insolence to a fat man wheezing.

'Break wind' in bawdy register also means to fart, and that secondary meaning, available to an Elizabethan audience, adds a deliberately deflating note to the grand senators' dignity — their 'insolence' is reduced to bodily ignominy. Whether Shakespeare intends the bawdy pun here is uncertain, but 'his wind' (the insolence personified as male) keeps it in play.

anchor_text: by the hazard of the spotted die Let die the spotted
summary: The Second Senator proposes leaving the selection of victims to the throw of a marked ('spotted') die — and lets 'the spotted' (those morally stained with guilt) be the ones who die. The compressed pun turns the spots of a gambling die into the moral spots of guilt, making a game of chance into a form of divine judgment.
detail: A die's spots (pips) are its identifying marks; 'spotted' as a moral term means stained, disgraced, guilty (compare 'spotless' reputation). The sentence enacts the very randomness it describes: the single word 'spotted' means both the physical marks on the die and the moral contamination of the condemned. 'Hazard' reinforces the gambling register — hazard was a popular Elizabethan dice game, and 'hazard' meant both risk and the game itself. The rhetorical device is antanaclasis, using the same word in two senses within one clause.

anchor_text: Against our rampir'd gates
summary: 'Rampir'd' means fortified with a rampart — a defensive earthwork or wall. The First Senator tells Alcibiades that merely setting his foot against their ramparted gates will be enough to open them, provided he sends his goodwill ahead: military force need not be used at all.
detail: The word is a participial form of 'rampire' (rampart), from French rempart. Its use here emphasizes the paradox: the senators describe their defences only to say they will immediately yield. The heavy fortification imagery (walls, gates, rampart) has run throughout the scene — the senators speak from the battlements above — and the First Senator dismantles it all rhetorically in a single clause, conceding that Alcibiades's soft approach is more powerful than his army.

anchor_text: to atone your fears With my more noble meaning
summary: 'Atone' here does not mean 'to make amends' (its modern sense) but its older meaning: to bring into agreement, to reconcile, to set at one. Alcibiades says he will reconcile ('at-one') their fears with the reality of his peaceful intentions.
detail: In Shakespeare 'atone' regularly means 'to reconcile persons or things that are at odds' — it is the verbal form of 'at one,' i.e., to make two parties one in agreement. The modern sense of making amends for a wrong developed later. Understanding the Elizabethan meaning is essential here: Alcibiades is not apologising for anything but explaining that his stated intentions ('noble meaning') will prove his fears groundless, bringing the two sides into agreement. The same usage appears at Richard II 1.1.202 ('To atone your royal self and your subjects') and Othello 4.1.234.

anchor_text: Here lies a wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft
summary: Timon's epitaph — 'Here lies a wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft... Here lie I, Timon, who alive all living men did hate' — is drawn from two real epitaphs that Plutarch records in his Life of Antony. Timon wrote them himself, insisting that even in death he wants no mourners, only curses.
detail: Plutarch (Life of Antony 70, in North's 1579 translation) preserves two epitaphs said to have been on Timon's tomb: one beginning 'Here lies a wretched corse' (a couplet attributed to Timon himself), the other 'Here lie I, Timon, who alive all living men did hate' (which Plutarch credits to the poet Callimachus). Shakespeare's four-line version conflates both. The contradiction - 'Seek not my name' immediately before 'Here lie I, Timon' - is inherited from the tradition and was noticed by early editors; it enacts Timon's self-contradicting nature: he cannot stop asserting himself even from beyond the grave. The stage direction 'ALCIBIADES reads the Epitaph' also follows Plutarch, who records the tomb by the sea.

anchor_text: use the olive with my sword, Make war breed peace
summary: The olive branch was the universal classical symbol of peace — an ambassador or herald carrying one declared peaceful intentions. Alcibiades combines it with his sword: he will enter Athens as both conqueror and peacemaker, with war and peace working together rather than cancelling each other. The closing formula — 'Make war breed peace, make peace stint war, make each / Prescribe to other, as each other's leech' — presents military force and civil order as physicians to each other.
detail: In Greek and Roman practice the olive was sacred to Athena (Minerva), patron of Athens itself, and was the emblem of peaceful negotiation and of the city's own identity (according to tradition Athens received its name and the olive tree from Athena, beating Poseidon). Using the olive alongside the sword in the city Athena founded has a quiet mythological fitness: Alcibiades re-enters as both soldier and Athenian citizen, restoring the balance Timon's cursing rage could never achieve. 'Stint' means restrain or check; 'leech' means physician (from Old English laece). The final couplet argues for a balanced, reciprocal constitution of force and peace — a civic resolution that closes the play's private tragedy on a public note. This resolution is Plutarchan: in Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades, he re-entered Athens in a mood of reconciliation.
